note: Hand-authored per-sentence analysis for the Omdat topic. Status ai-editorial-checked is not native-speaker review.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: It gives the real reason for working from home: a fact about the train, stated as a cause.

pat-omdat-01.situationNl: Een collega merkt dat je vandaag niet naar kantoor bent gekomen. Er is iets mis met het openbaar vervoer. Leg het uit.
pat-omdat-01.situationEn: A colleague notices you did not come to the office today, and public transport is the problem. Explain your reason.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik opens the sentence, so 'werk' is second. 'Thuis' says where.

clauses.subject: de trein
clauses.why: 'Niet' stands before the finite verb 'rijdt', which closes the dependent clause. As a main clause it would be 'De trein rijdt niet'.

pat-omdat-01.meaning: You say that you work from home today, and you give the cause: the train is not running.
pat-omdat-01.order: The main clause comes first and starts with its subject, so no inversion is needed. After omdat the clause turns into a dependent clause: the subject 'de trein' comes first, then 'niet', and the finite verb 'rijdt' moves to the very end.
pat-omdat-01.forms: werken: ik werk. rijden: de trein rijdt (-t for third person singular). 'Thuis' is a place adverb, not a noun. De trein is a de-word.
pat-omdat-01.compare: English 'because the train is not running' keeps 'is not running' together after the subject. Dutch puts 'niet' before the verb and the verb last: 'de trein niet rijdt'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik werk thuis omdat de trein rijdt niet.
mistakes.right: Ik werk thuis omdat de trein niet rijdt.
mistakes.why: 'De trein rijdt niet' is main-clause order. After omdat the negation comes before the verb, which ends the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik werk thuis omdat de trein niet rijden.
mistakes.right: Ik werk thuis omdat de trein niet rijdt.
mistakes.why: The verb must agree with the singular subject 'de trein': rijdt.

contrast.dutch: Ik werk thuis, want de trein rijdt niet.
contrast.english: I work from home, for the train is not running.
contrast.note: With 'want' the second part is a main clause again: 'de trein rijdt niet' keeps the verb second, unlike after omdat.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The broken computer is the cause of the call to the helpdesk, presented as a plain fact.

pat-omdat-02.situationNl: Je computer start niet meer op en je werk ligt stil. Vertel aan een collega wie je contacteert en wat de reden is.
pat-omdat-02.situationEn: Your computer no longer starts and your work has stopped. Tell a colleague who you are contacting and the reason.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'bel' is second; 'de helpdesk' is the object.

clauses.subject: mijn computer
clauses.why: 'Werken' means to function here. 'Niet' stands before 'werkt', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-02.meaning: You explain that you are phoning the helpdesk because your computer is faulty.
pat-omdat-02.order: Both clauses are short. The main clause is subject first, the dependent clause ends in 'werkt'. Because the dependent clause comes last, the main clause does not need to change anything.
pat-omdat-02.forms: bellen: ik bel (a transitive verb here: you call the helpdesk). werken: mijn computer werkt. 'Niet werken' = not working; the helpdesk is a de-word.
pat-omdat-02.compare: English 'my computer does not work' needs 'does'; Dutch has no do-support, only 'niet werkt'. English 'I am calling' becomes the simple present 'ik bel'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel de helpdesk omdat mijn computer werkt niet.
mistakes.right: Ik bel de helpdesk omdat mijn computer niet werkt.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb goes last, behind 'niet'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel de helpdesk omdat mijn computer niet doet werken.
mistakes.right: Ik bel de helpdesk omdat mijn computer niet werkt.
mistakes.why: Dutch does not use 'doen' as an auxiliary for negation; the lexical verb 'werkt' stands alone.

contrast.dutch: Omdat mijn computer niet werkt, bel ik de helpdesk.
contrast.english: Because my computer does not work, I am calling the helpdesk.
contrast.note: Reason first: the whole omdat-clause takes position one, so the main verb inverts to 'bel ik'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The expired password explains why logging in fails; omdat marks it as the reason.

pat-omdat-03.situationNl: Je probeert al een kwartier in te loggen, maar het systeem laat je niet toe. Leg aan de helpdesk uit wat de oorzaak is.
pat-omdat-03.situationEn: You have been trying to log in for fifteen minutes, but the system will not let you in. Tell the helpdesk what the cause is.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: The modal 'kan' is second; the infinitive 'inloggen' stays joined and closes the main clause, after 'niet'.

clauses.subject: mijn wachtwoord
clauses.why: 'Is verlopen' is a perfect-style group (is + participle) at the end of the dependent clause. Dutch also allows 'verlopen is'; this card uses 'is verlopen'.

pat-omdat-03.meaning: You report that you cannot log in, and why: your password has expired.
pat-omdat-03.order: The main clause has a modal and an infinitive, so 'inloggen' goes to the end of that clause. In the dependent clause the group 'is verlopen' closes the sentence. Verlopen takes zijn: the thing has run out by itself.
pat-omdat-03.forms: inloggen = in + loggen. After a modal it is joined. verlopen (to expire) forms its perfect with zijn: het wachtwoord is verlopen. The participle has no ge- because verlopen has an inseparable prefix ver-.
pat-omdat-03.compare: English 'my password has expired' uses 'has', Dutch 'is verlopen' uses zijn because the verb describes a change of state. English 'log in' keeps the particle after the verb; Dutch joins it after a modal.

mistakes.wrong: Ik kan niet in loggen omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen.
mistakes.right: Ik kan niet inloggen omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen.
mistakes.why: After a modal the separable verb stays joined: inloggen.

mistakes.wrong: Ik kan niet inloggen omdat mijn wachtwoord heeft verlopen.
mistakes.right: Ik kan niet inloggen omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen.
mistakes.why: Verlopen uses 'zijn' as its auxiliary, not 'hebben'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen, kan ik niet inloggen.
contrast.english: Because my password has expired, I cannot log in.
contrast.note: Reason first: the clause fills position one, so the modal 'kan' comes before 'ik', and the infinitive still ends the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The cold weather is the cause that makes you take a coat.

pat-omdat-04.situationNl: Je staat klaar om de deur uit te gaan en kijkt naar de thermometer. Zeg wat je meeneemt en wat daarvan de aanleiding is.
pat-omdat-04.situationEn: You are about to leave and look at the thermometer. Say what you take with you and the cause.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Meenemen is separable: 'neem ... mee'. The object 'een jas' stands between the verb and the particle 'mee'.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: 'Het' is the empty weather subject. The predicate 'koud' comes before the finite verb 'is', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-04.meaning: You say that you bring a coat, because it is cold.
pat-omdat-04.order: The main clause splits the separable verb around the object: neem ... mee. The dependent clause is the simplest pattern, predicate before the finite verb: koud is. Nothing precedes 'Ik', so there is no inversion.
pat-omdat-04.forms: meenemen = mee + nemen: ik neem mee, perfect: ik heb meegenomen. nemen is irregular in the stem (neem). 'Jas' is a de-word: een jas.
pat-omdat-04.compare: English 'take a coat with me' puts the object between 'take' and 'with'; Dutch 'neem een jas mee' leaves 'mee' at the end. English 'it is cold' keeps 'is' next to 'it'; Dutch moves it behind 'koud'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik neem een jas mee omdat het is koud.
mistakes.right: Ik neem een jas mee omdat het koud is.
mistakes.why: 'Het is koud' is main-clause order. After omdat the verb 'is' comes last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik meeneem een jas omdat het koud is.
mistakes.right: Ik neem een jas mee omdat het koud is.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'neem' second, 'mee' last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het koud is, neem ik een jas mee.
contrast.english: Because it is cold, I take a coat.
contrast.note: Reason first: the omdat-clause is position one, so 'neem' comes before 'ik', and the particle 'mee' still ends the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The colleague holding the key is the reason the group must wait.

pat-omdat-05.situationNl: Jullie staan met een groepje voor een gesloten lokaal. Een collega heeft de sleutel nog niet gebracht. Zeg namens iedereen wat jullie doen en waarom.
pat-omdat-05.situationEn: You stand with a small group in front of a locked room, and a colleague has not brought the key. Say, for everyone, what you are doing and why.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so 'wachten' is second. 'Wachten op' (to wait for) takes the preposition 'op'.

clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: 'Zij' is the colleague (she). The object 'de sleutel' stands before the finite verb 'heeft', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-05.meaning: You say, for the group, that you are waiting for a colleague, because she holds the key.
pat-omdat-05.order: The main clause is subject-first, with the preposition phrase 'op onze collega' after the verb. The dependent clause puts the object before the finite verb 'heeft'. Both clauses are short enough to see the pattern at a glance.
pat-omdat-05.forms: wachten op iemand = to wait for someone. hebben: zij heeft (-t). 'Onze collega' for a woman is still 'collega' (the word has no feminine form); 'zij' shows she is female.
pat-omdat-05.compare: English 'waiting for' needs 'for'; Dutch needs 'op'. English 'because she has the key' keeps 'has' before the object; Dutch puts 'heeft' last.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten op onze collega omdat zij heeft de sleutel.
mistakes.right: We wachten op onze collega omdat zij de sleutel heeft.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes behind the object.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten voor onze collega omdat zij de sleutel heeft.
mistakes.right: We wachten op onze collega omdat zij de sleutel heeft.
mistakes.why: Wachten takes 'op' for the person or thing waited for.

contrast.dutch: Omdat zij de sleutel heeft, wachten we op onze collega.
contrast.english: Because she has the key, we are waiting for our colleague.
contrast.note: Reason first: the clause fills position one and the main verb inverts to 'wachten we'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The illness explains the missed meeting, in the past.

pat-omdat-06.situationNl: Gisteren was er een belangrijke vergadering, maar je was er niet. Je manager vraagt hoe dat kwam. Antwoord.
pat-omdat-06.situationEn: There was an important meeting yesterday, but you were not there, and your manager asks how that happened. Answer.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: A perfect: the finite auxiliary 'heb' is second and the participle 'gemist' ends the main clause, behind the object 'de vergadering'.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Ziek' is the predicate and stands before the past verb 'was', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-06.meaning: You explain that you missed the meeting because you were ill.
pat-omdat-06.order: The main clause uses the perfect, so the verb pair is split: 'heb' in position two and 'gemist' at the end. The dependent clause uses the simple past 'was', after 'ziek'. Switching between perfect and simple past is normal: the perfect reports the event, the past gives the background state.
pat-omdat-06.forms: missen > gemist (perfect with hebben). zijn, simple past: ik was. Using the perfect for the missed meeting and the simple past for the state 'ziek was' is the usual pattern in speech.
pat-omdat-06.compare: English 'I missed' and 'I was ill' are both simple past. Dutch tends to use the perfect for the completed event (heb gemist) and the simple past for the state (was).

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb gemist de vergadering omdat ik ziek was.
mistakes.right: Ik heb de vergadering gemist omdat ik ziek was.
mistakes.why: In the perfect the participle goes to the end of the main clause, after the object.

mistakes.wrong: Ik heb de vergadering gemist omdat ik was ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik heb de vergadering gemist omdat ik ziek was.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes behind the predicate.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik ziek was, heb ik de vergadering gemist.
contrast.english: Because I was ill, I missed the meeting.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'heb ik', and the participle 'gemist' stays at the end.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Being ill is the reason for staying at home today.

pat-omdat-07.situationNl: Je hebt koorts en blijft vandaag in je woning. Een collega belt je op en vraagt wat er aan de hand is.
pat-omdat-07.situationEn: You have a fever and are staying indoors today. A colleague phones you and asks what is going on.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'blijf' is simply second; 'thuis' (at home) follows it.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Ik ben ziek' becomes 'omdat ik ziek ben': the predicate 'ziek' moves ahead of the finite verb 'ben', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-07.meaning: You tell a colleague that you are staying at home because you are ill.
pat-omdat-07.order: This is the cleanest omdat sentence: a normal main clause, then omdat, subject, predicate and the finite verb last. The finite verb 'ben' is the last word, and it takes the place that 'ben' would never have in a main clause ('Ik ben ziek').
pat-omdat-07.forms: blijven: ik blijf. zijn: ik ben. 'Ziek' is a predicate adjective and is not inflected after 'ben'.
pat-omdat-07.compare: English 'because I am ill' keeps 'am' second. Dutch reorders to 'ik ziek ben'. This is the first reordering an English speaker must learn, so it is worth repeating until it is automatic.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ben ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
mistakes.why: 'Ik ben ziek' is main-clause order; the dependent clause needs the verb at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis omdat ben ik ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
mistakes.why: Inversion belongs to main clauses only; omdat is followed by subject first.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik ziek ben, blijf ik thuis.
contrast.english: Because I am ill, I stay at home.
contrast.note: Reason first: the clause takes position one, so 'blijf' precedes 'ik' in the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The train delay is the cause of the colleague's later arrival.

pat-omdat-08.situationNl: Een collega zou er al moeten zijn, maar zijn trein rijdt niet zoals gepland. Je krijgt zijn bericht en meldt het aan de rest.
pat-omdat-08.situationEn: A colleague should already be here, but his train is not running as planned. You receive his message and tell the others.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'komt' is second; 'later' (later) follows it.

clauses.subject: de trein
clauses.why: 'Vertraging hebben' (to be delayed) puts the noun 'vertraging' before the finite verb 'heeft'.

pat-omdat-08.meaning: You report that she will be late, because her train is delayed.
pat-omdat-08.order: A main clause with a time adverb comes first. The dependent clause has the shape subject, object, finite verb. 'Vertraging heeft' is a fixed expression whose noun stays in front of the verb.
pat-omdat-08.forms: komen: zij komt. 'Vertraging hebben' = to be delayed; the noun has no article. Trein is a de-word.
pat-omdat-08.compare: English says 'the train is delayed' with a participle. Dutch says the train 'has delay' (vertraging heeft). Copying the English verb would lead to the mistake below.

mistakes.wrong: Zij komt later omdat de trein vertraging hebben.
mistakes.right: Zij komt later omdat de trein vertraging heeft.
mistakes.why: The verb must agree with the singular subject 'de trein': heeft, not the plural or infinitive form 'hebben'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij komt later omdat de trein heeft vertraging.
mistakes.right: Zij komt later omdat de trein vertraging heeft.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'heeft' goes behind the noun 'vertraging'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de trein vertraging heeft, komt zij later.
contrast.english: Because the train is delayed, she is coming later.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts to 'komt zij'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The rain explains the choice of bus over bicycle.

pat-omdat-09.situationNl: Je fiets staat in de gang en je gaat toch met het openbaar vervoer. Een buur vraagt hoe dat komt.
pat-omdat-09.situationEn: Your bike stands in the hallway and you are using public transport anyway. A neighbour asks why.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so 'nemen' (plural) is second; 'de bus' is the object.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: A weather clause of two words: the empty subject 'het' plus the verb 'regent', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-09.meaning: You say that you take the bus, because it is raining.
pat-omdat-09.order: Both clauses have a single verb, so the sentence is a good first drill. The main clause is subject-first, and the dependent clause has the order 'het regent' with the verb in last position, which here looks identical to the main clause because nothing else stands in the clause.
pat-omdat-09.forms: nemen: wij nemen (-en for plural). regenen: het regent. De bus is a de-word.
pat-omdat-09.compare: English 'because it is raining' uses 'is raining'; Dutch simply says 'het regent'. The order is the same here, but only because there is no other word in the clause; add an adverb and the verb moves to the end.

mistakes.wrong: We nemen de bus omdat regent het.
mistakes.right: We nemen de bus omdat het regent.
mistakes.why: The subject comes first after omdat; verb-before-subject belongs to main clauses.

mistakes.wrong: We neemt de bus omdat het regent.
mistakes.right: We nemen de bus omdat het regent.
mistakes.why: With the plural subject 'we' the verb ends in -en.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het regent, nemen we de bus.
contrast.english: Because it is raining, we take the bus.
contrast.note: Reason first: 'nemen we' is the inverted main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Working here is the reason he learns Dutch: a purpose-like but factual cause.

pat-omdat-10.situationNl: Je Poolse collega volgt sinds kort avondlessen. Een andere collega is benieuwd naar zijn motivatie. Geef een antwoord.
pat-omdat-10.situationEn: Your Polish colleague has recently started evening classes. Another colleague wonders about his motivation. Answer.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so 'leert' is second; 'Nederlands' is the object.

clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: The place adverb 'hier' stands before the finite verb 'werkt', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-10.meaning: You say that he is learning Dutch because he works here.
pat-omdat-10.order: In the main clause the object 'Nederlands' follows the verb. In the dependent clause 'hier' comes before 'werkt', so the last word is the finite verb. Note that 'hier' is not at the end, although it is the last non-verb word.
pat-omdat-10.forms: leren: hij leert. werken: hij werkt. 'Nederlands' (the language) is written with a capital N and has no article here.
pat-omdat-10.compare: English 'because he works here' keeps 'works' before 'here'; Dutch puts the verb last: 'hier werkt'. English 'learns Dutch' is the same order as Dutch.

mistakes.wrong: Hij leert Nederlands omdat hij werkt hier.
mistakes.right: Hij leert Nederlands omdat hij hier werkt.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the finite verb goes behind the place adverb.

mistakes.wrong: Hij leert Nederlands omdat hij hier werk.
mistakes.right: Hij leert Nederlands omdat hij hier werkt.
mistakes.why: With the subject 'hij' the finite verb takes -t: hij werkt.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij hier werkt, leert hij Nederlands.
contrast.english: Because he works here, he is learning Dutch.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts to 'leert hij'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The question is the reason for the call, which is the first thing you tell the person you phone.

pat-omdat-11.situationNl: Je belt een collega op die je niet vaak spreekt. Hij neemt op en je zegt direct waarom je belt.
pat-omdat-11.situationEn: You phone a colleague you rarely speak to. He picks up and you immediately say why you are calling.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'bel' is second; 'je' is the person you are calling.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The object 'een vraag' stands before the finite verb 'heb', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-11.meaning: You tell the person you phone that the reason for the call is that you have a question.
pat-omdat-11.order: The call comes first in the sentence, then the reason. The reason clause has object, then finite verb. Because both clauses start with 'ik', the learner must notice that the second 'ik' belongs to a dependent clause.
pat-omdat-11.forms: bellen: ik bel (to phone someone, with a direct object). hebben: ik heb. 'Een vraag hebben' = to have a question.
pat-omdat-11.compare: English 'because I have a question' keeps 'have' before 'a question'. Dutch reverses this: 'een vraag heb'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel je omdat ik heb een vraag.
mistakes.right: Ik bel je omdat ik een vraag heb.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'heb' goes behind its object.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel je omdat ik een vraag hebben.
mistakes.right: Ik bel je omdat ik een vraag heb.
mistakes.why: With the subject 'ik' the finite verb 'heb' has no ending and is not an infinitive.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik een vraag heb, bel ik je.
contrast.english: Because I have a question, I am calling you.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts to 'bel ik'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Little sleep is the cause of her tiredness: a past event explaining a present state.

pat-omdat-12.situationNl: Een vriendin gaapt de hele ochtend. Je collega vraagt je wat er met haar is. Geef de verklaring.
pat-omdat-12.situationEn: A friend yawns all morning, and a colleague asks you what is wrong with her. Give the explanation.

clauses.subject: Ze
clauses.why: Ze is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'is' is second; the predicate 'moe' (tired) follows it.

clauses.text: omdat ze vannacht weinig heeft geslapen
clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: A perfect: 'heeft geslapen' is the verb group at the end, behind 'vannacht' and 'weinig'. The finite 'heeft' is not the last word here.

pat-omdat-12.meaning: You say that she is tired because she slept little last night.
pat-omdat-12.order: The main clause is a simple statement of state. The dependent clause is longer: its adverbs 'vannacht' and 'weinig' come first and the perfect group 'heeft geslapen' closes it. This sentence shows that omdat clauses often end in a group of two verbs rather than a single verb.
pat-omdat-12.forms: slapen > geslapen (perfect with hebben). 'Vannacht' = last night (or tonight, from context). 'Weinig' = little (quantity). 'Ze' is the unstressed form of 'zij'.
pat-omdat-12.compare: English 'she slept little last night' uses the simple past. Dutch usually reports a finished event with the perfect, 'heeft geslapen', and puts the group at the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ze is moe omdat ze heeft vannacht weinig geslapen.
mistakes.right: Ze is moe omdat ze vannacht weinig heeft geslapen.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the auxiliary stays with the participle at the end of the clause, behind the adverbs.

mistakes.wrong: Ze is moe omdat ze vannacht weinig geslapen.
mistakes.right: Ze is moe omdat ze vannacht weinig heeft geslapen.
mistakes.why: A participle needs its auxiliary 'heeft' in the clause.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ze vannacht weinig heeft geslapen, is ze moe.
contrast.english: Because she slept little last night, she is tired.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'is ze moe'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The crowd explains why the group left early: the reason lies in the past, like the action itself.

pat-omdat-13.situationNl: Je vertelt over een uitstap waarbij jullie niet de hele avond bleven. Iemand vraagt waarom jullie eerder weggingen.
pat-omdat-13.situationEn: You are telling about an outing where you did not stay all evening. Someone asks why you left early.

clauses.subject: Wij
clauses.why: A perfect with zijn: 'zijn' is second and the participle 'vertrokken' ends the main clause.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: The empty subject 'het' and the predicate 'druk' come before the past verb 'was'.

pat-omdat-13.meaning: You say that you left early because it was crowded.
pat-omdat-13.order: The main clause has the perfect with zijn, so the pair 'zijn ... vertrokken' wraps around the adverb 'vroeg'. The dependent clause is in the simple past with the predicate before 'was'. The two tenses together report an event and its background.
pat-omdat-13.forms: vertrekken > vertrokken, perfect with zijn (a movement away). druk zijn = to be busy or crowded. 'Vroeg' = early.
pat-omdat-13.compare: English 'we left early because it was busy' uses the simple past twice. Dutch prefers the perfect for the departure, 'zijn vertrokken', and the simple past for the situation, 'was'.

mistakes.wrong: Wij hebben vroeg vertrokken omdat het druk was.
mistakes.right: Wij zijn vroeg vertrokken omdat het druk was.
mistakes.why: Vertrekken forms the perfect with zijn, not hebben.

mistakes.wrong: Wij zijn vroeg vertrokken omdat het was druk.
mistakes.right: Wij zijn vroeg vertrokken omdat het druk was.
mistakes.why: After omdat the predicate comes before the finite verb.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het druk was, zijn wij vroeg vertrokken.
contrast.english: Because it was busy, we left early.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'zijn wij', and the participle still ends it.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The expected rain is the cause for taking an umbrella: a reason based on a forecast.

pat-omdat-14.situationNl: De lucht wordt donker en je pakt je spullen in. Een collega ziet je iets extra meenemen. Zeg wat en waarom.
pat-omdat-14.situationEn: The sky is getting dark while you pack your things, and a colleague sees you take something extra. Say what and why.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Meenemen is separable: 'neem ... mee' wraps around the object 'een paraplu'.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: 'Gaat regenen' is a verb group: the finite 'gaat' plus the infinitive 'regenen' (going to rain), so the clause ends with the infinitive.

pat-omdat-14.meaning: You say that you bring an umbrella because rain is on the way.
pat-omdat-14.order: The main clause wraps around its object: neem ... mee. The dependent clause is a verb group: the finite 'gaat' stands directly before the infinitive 'regenen', and together they close the clause. This is the Dutch near future: gaan plus infinitive.
pat-omdat-14.forms: gaan + infinitive expresses what is about to happen: het gaat regenen. meenemen: ik neem mee. 'Paraplu' is a de-word.
pat-omdat-14.compare: English 'it is going to rain' keeps 'is going to rain' together after 'it'. In Dutch the group also stays together, but it moves to the end of the omdat clause: 'omdat het gaat regenen'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik neem een paraplu mee omdat het gaat regent.
mistakes.right: Ik neem een paraplu mee omdat het gaat regenen.
mistakes.why: After gaan the second verb is an infinitive: gaat regenen. A finite 'regent' cannot follow 'gaat'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik meeneem een paraplu omdat het gaat regenen.
mistakes.right: Ik neem een paraplu mee omdat het gaat regenen.
mistakes.why: In a main clause the separable verb splits; 'neem' is second and 'mee' goes last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het gaat regenen, neem ik een paraplu mee.
contrast.english: Because it is going to rain, I take an umbrella.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'neem ik ... mee'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The public holiday is the reason the shop is closed: an explanation you give to someone who does not know.

pat-omdat-15.situationNl: Een toerist staat voor een gesloten winkel en snapt het niet. Leg hem uit wat er aan de hand is.
pat-omdat-15.situationEn: A tourist stands in front of a closed shop and does not understand. Explain what is going on.

clauses.subject: De winkel
clauses.why: The subject comes first, so 'is' is second; 'dicht' (closed) is the predicate.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: 'Het is feestdag' (it is a holiday) becomes 'omdat het feestdag is'. The noun 'feestdag' is the predicate and stands before 'is'.

pat-omdat-15.meaning: You explain that the shop is closed because it is a public holiday.
pat-omdat-15.order: Both clauses contain 'is', but in different places. In the main clause 'is' is second; in the dependent clause it is last. Comparing the two is a quick way to see the difference between main and dependent order.
pat-omdat-15.forms: zijn: is in both clauses. 'Feestdag' is a de-word (de feestdag) and acts as a predicate noun after 'is'. 'Dicht' is the usual word for closed shops.
pat-omdat-15.compare: English 'because it is a holiday' keeps 'is' next to 'it'. Dutch shows the clause is dependent by pushing 'is' to the end: 'het feestdag is'.

mistakes.wrong: De winkel is dicht omdat het is feestdag.
mistakes.right: De winkel is dicht omdat het feestdag is.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb 'is' goes to the end of the clause, behind the predicate noun 'feestdag'.

mistakes.wrong: De winkel is dicht omdat het feestdag zijn.
mistakes.right: De winkel is dicht omdat het feestdag is.
mistakes.why: The subject 'het' is singular, so the dependent clause needs 'is' and not the plural 'zijn'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het feestdag is, is de winkel dicht.
contrast.english: Because it is a holiday, the shop is closed.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'is de winkel dicht', so the two forms of 'is' now stand next to each other's clauses.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: An obligation to work is the reason he cannot come.

pat-omdat-16.situationNl: Een vriend zou meekomen naar een etentje, maar hij laat het je vandaag weten. Jij geeft zijn verklaring door aan de groep.
pat-omdat-16.situationEn: A friend was going to join a dinner but sent a message today. You pass his explanation on to the group.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: The modal 'kan' is second and the infinitive 'komen' ends the main clause, behind 'niet'.

clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: 'Moet werken' is a modal group at the end of the dependent clause: the finite 'moet' plus the infinitive 'werken'.

pat-omdat-16.meaning: You say that he cannot come, because he has to work.
pat-omdat-16.order: Both clauses have a modal and an infinitive. The main clause keeps the usual order: modal second, infinitive last. The dependent clause keeps the verbs together at the end, and the finite modal 'moet' stands directly before 'werken'.
pat-omdat-16.forms: kunnen: hij kan. moeten: hij moet. After a modal Dutch uses a bare infinitive: kan komen, moet werken. 'Have to' becomes 'moeten', not 'hebben'.
pat-omdat-16.compare: English 'he has to work' uses 'has to'. Dutch uses the modal 'moet' with a bare infinitive. English 'because he has to work' keeps the verbs in a row; Dutch does too, but at the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Hij kan niet komen omdat hij heeft te werken.
mistakes.right: Hij kan niet komen omdat hij moet werken.
mistakes.why: Necessity is expressed with 'moeten' plus an infinitive, not 'hebben te'.

mistakes.wrong: Hij kan niet komen omdat hij moet werken te.
mistakes.right: Hij kan niet komen omdat hij moet werken.
mistakes.why: A modal takes the bare infinitive, without 'te'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij moet werken, kan hij niet komen.
contrast.english: Because he has to work, he cannot come.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'kan hij niet komen', with the infinitive still last.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The coming visitors are the reason you are cleaning up now.

pat-omdat-17.situationNl: Je loopt met een stofzuiger door je woonkamer. Een huisgenoot vraagt waarom je zo druk bent.
pat-omdat-17.situationEn: You are walking through your living room with a vacuum cleaner. A housemate asks why you are so busy.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Opruimen (to tidy up) is separable: 'ruim ... op'. With no object, the particle follows the verb directly.

clauses.subject: bezoek
clauses.why: 'Er' introduces the indefinite subject 'bezoek' (visitors), and the finite verb 'komt' closes the clause.

pat-omdat-17.meaning: You say that you are tidying up because visitors are on their way.
pat-omdat-17.order: The main clause is two words long and shows the split of a separable verb: ruim ... op. In the dependent clause 'er' follows omdat directly, then the subject 'bezoek', then the verb 'komt' last.
pat-omdat-17.forms: opruimen: ik ruim op, perfect: ik heb opgeruimd. 'Bezoek' (visitors, a visit) is a het-word with no plural; the verb is singular 'komt'. 'Er komt bezoek' = visitors are coming.
pat-omdat-17.compare: English 'because visitors are coming' has no 'there'. Dutch usually adds 'er' before an indefinite subject. English 'tidy up' also has a particle, but it can sit directly after the verb; Dutch puts it at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ruim op omdat er komt bezoek.
mistakes.right: Ik ruim op omdat er bezoek komt.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'komt' goes last, behind the subject 'bezoek'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik opruim omdat er bezoek komt.
mistakes.right: Ik ruim op omdat er bezoek komt.
mistakes.why: In a main clause a separable verb splits: 'ruim' second, 'op' last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat er bezoek komt, ruim ik op.
contrast.english: Because visitors are coming, I am tidying up.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'ruim ik op', with the particle last.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The faulty printer is why the colleague is calling.

pat-omdat-18.situationNl: Er belt een collega van de eerste verdieping naar de kamer van je team. Je neemt op en zegt een collega waarover het gaat.
pat-omdat-18.situationEn: A colleague from the first floor is ringing your team's room. You pick up and tell another colleague what it is about.

clauses.subject: Mijn collega
clauses.why: The subject 'Mijn collega' is first, so 'belt' is second. No object follows.

clauses.subject: de printer
clauses.why: 'Niet' stands before the finite verb 'werkt', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-18.meaning: You say that your colleague is phoning because the printer is not working.
pat-omdat-18.order: A very short main clause is followed by a dependent clause of three words and a verb. The noun-phrase subject 'Mijn collega' opens the sentence, so no inversion. In the dependent clause 'niet' sits right before 'werkt'.
pat-omdat-18.forms: bellen: mijn collega belt (-t). werken (to function): de printer werkt. 'Printer' is a de-word. 'Bellen' without an object means to make a phone call.
pat-omdat-18.compare: English 'because the printer isn't working' has 'isn't' before 'working'; Dutch has just 'niet werkt'. English 'is phoning' is a continuous form; Dutch uses the simple present.

mistakes.wrong: Mijn collega belt omdat de printer werkt niet.
mistakes.right: Mijn collega belt omdat de printer niet werkt.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb goes behind the negation.

mistakes.wrong: Mijn collega belt omdat de printer is niet werken.
mistakes.right: Mijn collega belt omdat de printer niet werkt.
mistakes.why: Dutch does not use 'zijn' plus an infinitive for ongoing action; the simple present 'werkt' is enough.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de printer niet werkt, belt mijn collega.
contrast.english: Because the printer is not working, my colleague is phoning.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts to 'belt mijn collega', with the noun-phrase subject after the verb.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The doctor's being busy is the reason for the wait.

pat-omdat-19.situationNl: Je zit met een vriend in een wachtkamer en jullie worden steeds niet binnengeroepen. Hij vraagt waarom het zo lang duurt.
pat-omdat-19.situationEn: You sit with a friend in a waiting room and you are still not called in. He asks why it takes so long.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'wachten' is second; nothing else is needed.

clauses.text: omdat de dokter nog bezig is
clauses.subject: de dokter
clauses.why: 'Nog bezig' (still busy) stands before the finite verb 'is', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-19.meaning: You say that you are still waiting because the doctor is still busy.
pat-omdat-19.order: The main clause is just subject and verb. The dependent clause collects 'nog' and the predicate 'bezig' before 'is', so the sentence ends on 'is'. 'Nog' (still) is placed in front of the predicate.
pat-omdat-19.forms: wachten: wij wachten. 'Bezig zijn' = to be busy or occupied. 'Nog' means 'still' here. 'Dokter' is a de-word.
pat-omdat-19.compare: English 'the doctor is still busy' keeps 'is' before 'still busy'. Dutch moves it behind: 'nog bezig is'.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten omdat de dokter is nog bezig.
mistakes.right: We wachten omdat de dokter nog bezig is.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes after 'nog bezig'.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten omdat de dokter bezig nog is.
mistakes.right: We wachten omdat de dokter nog bezig is.
mistakes.why: The adverb 'nog' comes before the predicate it modifies, not after it.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de dokter nog bezig is, wachten we.
contrast.english: Because the doctor is still busy, we are waiting.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts to 'wachten we'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Missing the bus explains why she is cycling: a past event giving the present reason.

pat-omdat-20.situationNl: Je collega komt vandaag met de fiets aan hoewel ze meestal de bus neemt. Een andere collega is verbaasd. Vertel wat er gebeurd is.
pat-omdat-20.situationEn: Your colleague arrives by bike today although she usually takes the bus, and another colleague is surprised. Tell what happened.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'fietst' is second. The verb 'fietsen' has no object here.

clauses.text: omdat ze de bus heeft gemist
clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: A perfect: the object 'de bus' stands before the verb group 'heeft gemist', which ends the clause.

pat-omdat-20.meaning: You explain that she is cycling today, because she missed the bus.
pat-omdat-20.order: The main clause is in the present, the dependent clause in the perfect: that mix tells the story of cause and effect in time. The group 'heeft gemist' closes the sentence after the object.
pat-omdat-20.forms: fietsen: zij fietst. missen > gemist (perfect with hebben). 'De bus missen' = to miss the bus. 'Zij' and 'ze' are the stressed and unstressed forms of the same pronoun.
pat-omdat-20.compare: English 'because she missed the bus' is a simple past. Dutch here uses the perfect 'heeft gemist' to link a past event to the present situation.

mistakes.wrong: Zij fietst omdat ze heeft de bus gemist.
mistakes.right: Zij fietst omdat ze de bus heeft gemist.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the object comes before the perfect group.

mistakes.wrong: Zij fietst omdat ze de bus is gemist.
mistakes.right: Zij fietst omdat ze de bus heeft gemist.
mistakes.why: Missen forms its perfect with hebben: ze heeft de bus gemist, not 'is gemist'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ze de bus heeft gemist, fietst zij.
contrast.english: Because she missed the bus, she is cycling.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'fietst zij'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The rain is stated as the cause of staying in, and the reason comes first because it is the thing you want the listener to hear before the decision.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: The empty weather subject 'het' plus the verb 'regent', which closes the clause. With only two words, the clause looks like a main clause, but it is dependent.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The whole omdat-clause is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'blijf' has to come before 'ik'.

pat-omdat-21.meaning: You give the reason first (it is raining) and then the consequence: you stay at home.
pat-omdat-21.order: A fronted reason makes the dependent clause position one of the whole sentence. Dutch then requires the finite verb of the main clause immediately after it: blijf ik, not ik blijf.
pat-omdat-21.forms: regenen: het regent. blijven: ik blijf. 'Thuis' means at home as a place; 'naar huis' would be home as a direction.
pat-omdat-21.compare: English 'Because it is raining, I stay at home' keeps 'I stay' in subject-first order. Dutch has to say 'blijf ik'. That inversion is the most English-speakers' stumbling block with fronted omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het regent, ik blijf thuis.
mistakes.right: Omdat het regent, blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.why: A fronted dependent clause counts as the first constituent, so the main verb must come second, before 'ik'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat regent het, blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.right: Omdat het regent, blijf ik thuis.
mistakes.why: After omdat the subject comes first and the verb last; verb-before-subject belongs to the main clause.

contrast.dutch: Ik blijf thuis omdat het regent.
contrast.english: I stay at home because it is raining.
contrast.note: Main clause first: ordinary 'Ik blijf', and the reason follows without any inversion.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The delay is given as the explanation that a late arrival needs, before the announcement itself.

clauses.subject: de trein
clauses.why: 'Vertraging hebben' (to be delayed): the noun 'vertraging' comes before the finite verb 'heeft', which ends the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'kom' precedes 'ik'. 'Later' (later) follows the subject.

pat-omdat-22.meaning: You say that you will arrive later, and you start with the cause: the train is delayed.
pat-omdat-22.order: The reason clause ends in 'heeft', and as a whole it fills position one of the sentence. The main verb 'kom' therefore comes second, followed by its subject 'ik' and then 'later'.
pat-omdat-22.forms: komen: ik kom (no ending). hebben: de trein heeft. The expression 'vertraging hebben' needs no article. 'Later' is a comparative adverb meaning at a later time.
pat-omdat-22.compare: English says 'the train is delayed' with a participle; Dutch says the train 'has delay'. English 'I will be later' needs 'will be'; Dutch uses the present tense 'kom ik later'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de trein heeft vertraging, kom ik later.
mistakes.right: Omdat de trein vertraging heeft, kom ik later.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the object 'vertraging' stands before the finite verb, which is last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de trein vertraging heeft, ik kom later.
mistakes.right: Omdat de trein vertraging heeft, kom ik later.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause takes position one, so the main verb has to come before 'ik'.

contrast.dutch: Ik kom later omdat de trein vertraging heeft.
contrast.english: I will be later because the train is delayed.
contrast.note: Main clause first: the announcement comes before the cause, so 'Ik kom' keeps normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Illness is the reason for the change of working place; it is placed first to justify the plan.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Ik ben ziek' becomes 'omdat ik ziek ben': the predicate 'ziek' moves in front of the finite verb 'ben'.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'werk' precedes 'ik'. The time adverb 'vandaag' follows the subject; 'thuis' closes the clause.

pat-omdat-23.meaning: You tell your team that today you work from home, and the first thing they hear is the reason: you are ill.
pat-omdat-23.order: Two 'ik' phrases stand next to each other across the comma: the first ends the dependent clause, the second follows the inverted verb 'werk'. A time adverb like 'vandaag' stays behind the subject in the main clause.
pat-omdat-23.forms: zijn: ik ben. werken: ik werk. 'Vandaag' is a time adverb; it sits after the verb and subject, before the place 'thuis'.
pat-omdat-23.compare: English 'because I am ill, I am working from home today' uses 'am working'. Dutch uses the simple present 'werk ik'. English keeps 'I am' in order; Dutch puts 'ben' last in the first clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik ben ziek, werk ik vandaag thuis.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik ziek ben, werk ik vandaag thuis.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause 'ziek' has to stand in front of 'ben'; 'ik ben ziek' is the order of a main clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik ziek ben, ik werk vandaag thuis.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik ziek ben, werk ik vandaag thuis.
mistakes.why: The main verb comes right after the fronted dependent clause, before 'ik'.

contrast.dutch: Ik werk vandaag thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
contrast.english: I am working from home today because I am ill.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik werk vandaag thuis' in normal order, with the reason as a closing dependent clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The unresponsive server is the established reason for the check; this is a real cause, not a hypothesis.

clauses.subject: de server
clauses.why: 'Niet' stands before the finite verb 'reageert', which closes the dependent clause. 'De server reageert niet' would be the main-clause form.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause fills position one, so 'controleer' comes before 'ik'. 'De logs' is the object.

pat-omdat-24.meaning: You explain that you are checking the logs, because the server does not respond.
pat-omdat-24.order: 'Omdat de server niet reageert' is one constituent in position one. Dutch main clauses keep the finite verb in position two, so the next words are 'controleer ik'. The object 'de logs' closes the sentence.
pat-omdat-24.forms: reageren: de server reageert. controleren: ik controleer (no ge- in the participle because of the inseparable prefix; here a present form). 'De logs' is the plural of 'de log'.
pat-omdat-24.compare: English 'because the server isn't responding' contracts 'is not'. Dutch just has 'niet' before the verb. English keeps 'I am checking' in order; Dutch inverts to 'controleer ik'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de server reageert niet, controleer ik de logs.
mistakes.right: Omdat de server niet reageert, controleer ik de logs.
mistakes.why: After omdat 'niet' stands before the verb, which is last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de server niet reageert, ik controleer de logs.
mistakes.right: Omdat de server niet reageert, controleer ik de logs.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause counts as the first constituent; the main verb must be second.

contrast.dutch: Ik controleer de logs, want de server reageert niet.
contrast.english: I am checking the logs, for the server is not responding.
contrast.note: With 'want' two main clauses are joined, so the second one keeps the normal order 'de server reageert niet', with the verb second.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The incomplete form is the cause of your request for more details.

clauses.subject: het formulier
clauses.why: 'Onvolledig' (incomplete) is the predicate and stands before the finite verb 'is', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'vraag' comes before 'ik'. 'Extra gegevens' (extra data) is the object.

pat-omdat-25.meaning: You explain that you ask for extra information, because the form is incomplete.
pat-omdat-25.order: The predicate comes before 'is' in the reason clause. The clause then takes position one, so the main verb 'vraag' precedes 'ik'. Without an article, 'extra gegevens' is a general plural object.
pat-omdat-25.forms: vragen: ik vraag. 'Gegevens' is a plural-only noun (data, details). 'Het formulier' is a het-word. 'Onvolledig' is not inflected after 'is'.
pat-omdat-25.compare: English 'because the form is incomplete' keeps 'is' second. Dutch moves it to the end behind 'onvolledig'. English 'ask for' needs 'for'; Dutch 'vragen' takes the object directly here.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het formulier is onvolledig, vraag ik extra gegevens.
mistakes.right: Omdat het formulier onvolledig is, vraag ik extra gegevens.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'is' goes behind the predicate.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het formulier onvolledig is, ik vraag extra gegevens.
mistakes.right: Omdat het formulier onvolledig is, vraag ik extra gegevens.
mistakes.why: The fronted dependent clause makes the main verb come second.

contrast.dutch: Het formulier is onvolledig. Daarom vraag ik extra gegevens.
contrast.english: The form is incomplete. That is why I am asking for extra information.
contrast.note: With 'daarom' the result starts a new sentence; 'daarom' fills position one, so the verb still comes second: 'vraag ik'. Daarom is an adverb, not a conjunction.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The expired password is the cause of the failed login; the reason is stated first.

clauses.subject: mijn wachtwoord
clauses.why: 'Is verlopen' closes the clause (is + participle). Verlopen forms its perfect with zijn.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kan' precedes 'ik'. The infinitive 'inloggen' stays joined at the end, behind 'niet'.

pat-omdat-26.meaning: You explain that you cannot log in, starting with the cause: your password has expired.
pat-omdat-26.order: The reason clause ends in the group 'is verlopen'. The main clause then starts with the modal and the subject, and the infinitive 'inloggen' closes the sentence. A separable verb stays in one piece after a modal.
pat-omdat-26.forms: inloggen = in + loggen. After kunnen the infinitive is joined. verlopen > is verlopen (zijn). The same sentence in the other order, 'Ik kan niet inloggen omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen', is the legacy card.
pat-omdat-26.compare: English 'my password has expired' uses 'has'. Dutch says 'is verlopen' with zijn. English 'cannot log in' keeps the particle; Dutch 'inloggen' keeps it joined after the modal.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen, ik kan niet inloggen.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen, kan ik niet inloggen.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is the first constituent, so the modal verb has to come second.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen, kan ik niet loggen in.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen, kan ik niet inloggen.
mistakes.why: After a modal the separable verb is not split: inloggen.

contrast.dutch: Ik kan niet inloggen omdat mijn wachtwoord is verlopen.
contrast.english: I cannot log in because my password has expired.
contrast.note: Main clause first: ordinary 'Ik kan niet inloggen', then the reason clause with its verb group last.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The closed shop is the cause of the change of plan.

clauses.subject: de winkel
clauses.why: 'Dicht' (closed) is the predicate, and the finite verb 'is' closes the clause.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'gaan' precedes 'we'. 'Naar de markt' is the direction.

pat-omdat-27.meaning: You say that your plan changes (to the market) because the shop is closed.
pat-omdat-27.order: The two clauses each contain a verb that works with a predicate or direction: 'dicht is' and 'naar de markt'. The dependent clause comes first, so the main verb 'gaan' leads the main clause, followed by the plural subject 'we'.
pat-omdat-27.forms: gaan: wij gaan. 'Naar' with a place gives a direction: naar de markt. 'De winkel' is a de-word; 'de markt' too.
pat-omdat-27.compare: English 'we are going to the market' uses a continuous; Dutch uses the simple present. English keeps 'we are going' in order; Dutch must say 'gaan we'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de winkel is dicht, gaan we naar de markt.
mistakes.right: Omdat de winkel dicht is, gaan we naar de markt.
mistakes.why: 'Dicht' goes in front of 'is' once omdat has turned the clause into a dependent one: de winkel dicht is.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de winkel dicht is, we gaan naar de markt.
mistakes.right: Omdat de winkel dicht is, gaan we naar de markt.
mistakes.why: The main verb has to come second after a fronted dependent clause.

contrast.dutch: We gaan naar de markt omdat de winkel dicht is.
contrast.english: We are going to the market because the shop is closed.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'We gaan' in plain subject-first order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The missed bus is a past event that explains the lateness; it is given first as the excuse.

clauses.text: Omdat ik de bus heb gemist
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The object 'de bus' stands before the perfect group 'heb gemist', which ends the clause. 'Heb' is the finite verb but not the last word.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'kom' precedes 'ik'. 'Te laat' (too late) follows.

pat-omdat-28.meaning: You apologise for being late and start with the cause: you missed your bus.
pat-omdat-28.order: The perfect group 'heb gemist' closes the dependent clause behind its object. That clause is position one, so 'kom ik te laat' follows. The present tense 'kom' covers the near future.
pat-omdat-28.forms: missen > gemist (perfect with hebben). 'Te laat' = too late (a fixed phrase). komen: ik kom.
pat-omdat-28.compare: English 'because I missed the bus' uses the simple past. Dutch usually uses the perfect for a finished event with present relevance: 'heb gemist'. English says 'I will be late', Dutch simply 'kom ik te laat'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik heb de bus gemist, kom ik te laat.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik de bus heb gemist, kom ik te laat.
mistakes.why: The perfect group 'heb gemist' stands behind the object 'de bus' here; the auxiliary does not follow 'ik' directly after omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik de bus heb gemist, ik kom te laat.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik de bus heb gemist, kom ik te laat.
mistakes.why: After the fronted clause the main verb comes second.

contrast.dutch: Ik kom te laat omdat ik de bus heb gemist.
contrast.english: I will be late because I missed the bus.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik kom te laat' in normal order, then the reason.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: A colleague's illness is the reason you cover his work.

clauses.subject: mijn collega
clauses.why: 'Ziek' (ill) comes before the finite verb 'is', which ends the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'neem' precedes 'ik'. Overnemen (to take over) is separable, so the particle 'over' ends the clause after 'zijn taken'.

pat-omdat-29.meaning: You explain that you cover your ill colleague's tasks.
pat-omdat-29.order: The reason clause ends with 'is'. The main clause inverts to 'neem ik', and the separable verb leaves its particle 'over' at the end after the object. Two features meet here: inversion and a split verb.
pat-omdat-29.forms: overnemen = over + nemen: ik neem over, perfect: ik heb overgenomen. 'Zijn' in 'zijn taken' is the possessive (his); the verb 'is' is the other word. Taken is the plural of taak.
pat-omdat-29.compare: English 'take over his tasks' has the particle near the verb; Dutch has it last. English 'because my colleague is ill' keeps 'is' second; Dutch moves it to the end.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn collega ziek is, overneem ik zijn taken.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn collega ziek is, neem ik zijn taken over.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'neem' second, 'over' last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn collega is ziek, neem ik zijn taken over.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn collega ziek is, neem ik zijn taken over.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb goes behind the predicate.

contrast.dutch: Ik neem zijn taken over omdat mijn collega ziek is.
contrast.english: I am taking over his tasks because my colleague is ill.
contrast.note: Main clause first: the split verb 'neem ... over' keeps the particle last in the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The empty paper tray is the cause of the refill, stated first for someone who wonders what you are doing.

clauses.text: Omdat de printer geen papier meer heeft
clauses.subject: de printer
clauses.why: 'Geen papier meer' (no more paper) stands before the finite verb 'heeft', which closes the clause. 'Geen' negates the noun.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'vul' precedes 'ik'. Bijvullen is separable: the particle 'bij' ends the clause.

pat-omdat-30.meaning: You say that you are refilling the paper tray because the printer has run out of paper.
pat-omdat-30.order: The reason clause has its negated object in front of 'heeft'. The main clause inverts to 'vul ik', and the particle 'bij' closes the sentence after 'de lade'.
pat-omdat-30.forms: bijvullen = bij + vullen: ik vul bij. 'Geen ... meer' = no more. 'Lade' is a de-word. Dutch says the printer 'has no more paper' where English says it 'has run out'.
pat-omdat-30.compare: English 'has run out of paper' is a different structure; Dutch 'geen papier meer heeft' uses the verb 'hebben'. English 'refill the tray' has no particle; Dutch 'vul ... bij' ends with it.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de printer geen papier meer heeft, bijvul ik de lade.
mistakes.right: Omdat de printer geen papier meer heeft, vul ik de lade bij.
mistakes.why: In a main clause the separable verb splits; 'bij' goes last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de printer niet papier meer heeft, vul ik de lade bij.
mistakes.right: Omdat de printer geen papier meer heeft, vul ik de lade bij.
mistakes.why: A noun without an article is negated with 'geen', not 'niet'.

contrast.dutch: Ik vul de lade bij omdat de printer geen papier meer heeft.
contrast.english: I am refilling the tray because the printer has no paper left.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik vul ... bij' stays in normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The early start tomorrow is the reason for going to bed early tonight: a cause planned in advance.

clauses.text: Omdat ik morgen vroeg moet opstaan
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Moet opstaan' is a modal group: the finite 'moet' plus the joined infinitive 'opstaan'. They close the clause behind 'morgen vroeg'.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'ga' precedes 'ik'. After 'gaan' the infinitive 'slapen' ends the clause.

pat-omdat-31.meaning: You tell someone that you will go to bed early because you must get up early tomorrow.
pat-omdat-31.order: The dependent clause ends in a verb group where the separable verb 'opstaan' stays joined after the modal 'moet'. The main clause then inverts to 'ga ik' and ends with the infinitive 'slapen'. Two verb groups, one in each clause.
pat-omdat-31.forms: opstaan = op + staan. After a modal it is joined: moet opstaan. gaan + infinitive (ga slapen) says that you are going to sleep. 'Morgen vroeg' = early tomorrow.
pat-omdat-31.compare: English 'I have to get up' uses 'have to' and a phrasal verb. Dutch uses the modal 'moet' and the joined verb 'opstaan'. English 'go to bed' is a phrase; Dutch uses 'gaan slapen' (go to sleep).

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik morgen vroeg moet staan op, ga ik vroeg slapen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik morgen vroeg moet opstaan, ga ik vroeg slapen.
mistakes.why: A separable verb stays joined after a modal: opstaan.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik morgen vroeg moet opstaan, ik ga vroeg slapen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik morgen vroeg moet opstaan, ga ik vroeg slapen.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is position one, so 'ga' comes before 'ik'.

contrast.dutch: Ik ga vroeg slapen omdat ik morgen vroeg moet opstaan.
contrast.english: I am going to bed early because I have to get up early tomorrow.
contrast.note: Main clause first: ordinary 'Ik ga', with the infinitive 'slapen' ending the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Lack of time justifies the choice: the reason clause opens the sentence to support a decision.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: 'Weinig tijd hebben' (to have little time): the object 'weinig tijd' stands before the finite verb 'hebben', which ends the clause.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'kiezen' precedes 'we'. 'De snelste oplossing' is the object, a superlative.

pat-omdat-32.meaning: You justify choosing the quickest solution by saying that time is short.
pat-omdat-32.order: The dependent clause ends with the plural 'hebben'. After it, the main clause inverts to 'kiezen we', followed by the superlative object 'de snelste oplossing'.
pat-omdat-32.forms: hebben: wij hebben. kiezen: wij kiezen. snel > snelst: 'de snelste' is the superlative with -e before a de-word. Oplossing is a de-word.
pat-omdat-32.compare: English 'because we have little time' puts 'have' second; Dutch ends with it. English 'the fastest solution' needs 'the' plus -est; Dutch has the same shape: de snelste.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat we hebben weinig tijd, kiezen we de snelste oplossing.
mistakes.right: Omdat we weinig tijd hebben, kiezen we de snelste oplossing.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes behind its object.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat we weinig tijd hebben, we kiezen de snelste oplossing.
mistakes.right: Omdat we weinig tijd hebben, kiezen we de snelste oplossing.
mistakes.why: After the long fronted clause 'kiezen' has to open the main clause, with 'we' behind it.

contrast.dutch: We kiezen de snelste oplossing omdat we weinig tijd hebben.
contrast.english: We choose the fastest solution because we have little time.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'We kiezen' in subject-first order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The failed update is the cause of the rollback; it is placed first as the justification.

clauses.subject: de update
clauses.why: 'Mislukt is' is the group (participle before 'is'). Mislukken forms its perfect with zijn.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'draaien' precedes 'we'. Terugdraaien is separable: the particle 'terug' ends the clause.

pat-omdat-33.meaning: You say that you are reversing the change because the update failed.
pat-omdat-33.order: The dependent clause ends with the group 'mislukt is'. After it the main clause starts with the verb 'draaien' and ends with the particle 'terug', with the object between them.
pat-omdat-33.forms: mislukken > mislukt (zijn; the verb is inseparable). terugdraaien = terug + draaien. 'Is mislukt' and 'mislukt is' are both used; this card keeps the participle first.
pat-omdat-33.compare: English 'the update failed' is a plain past. Dutch uses the perfect 'is mislukt' for a failure with a present consequence. English 'roll back' has the particle after the verb or object; Dutch last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de update mislukt is, terugdraaien we de wijziging.
mistakes.right: Omdat de update mislukt is, draaien we de wijziging terug.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause; 'draaien' is second and 'terug' last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de update heeft mislukt, draaien we de wijziging terug.
mistakes.right: Omdat de update mislukt is, draaien we de wijziging terug.
mistakes.why: Mislukken takes zijn, not hebben, and the group closes the clause.

contrast.dutch: We draaien de wijziging terug omdat de update mislukt is.
contrast.english: We are rolling back the change because the update failed.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'We draaien ... terug'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Not understanding the explanation is the cause of your question.

clauses.text: Omdat ik de uitleg niet begrijp
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The object 'de uitleg' and 'niet' stand before the finite verb 'begrijp', which closes the clause. 'Begrijpen' is inseparable.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'stel' precedes 'ik'. 'Een vraag stellen' is the fixed way to ask a question.

pat-omdat-34.meaning: You say that you ask a question, since you do not understand the explanation.
pat-omdat-34.order: The object and the negation come before the verb in the first clause. The finished clause fills position one, so the main verb 'stel' leads before 'ik'. The sentence has two 'ik', one in each clause.
pat-omdat-34.forms: begrijpen: ik begrijp. stellen: ik stel. 'De uitleg' is a de-word (the explanation). 'Een vraag stellen' is a collocation.
pat-omdat-34.compare: English 'ask a question' uses 'ask'; Dutch uses 'stellen'. English 'I do not understand' uses 'do not'; Dutch puts 'niet' before the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik de uitleg begrijp niet, stel ik een vraag.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik de uitleg niet begrijp, stel ik een vraag.
mistakes.why: 'Niet' goes before the final verb in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik de uitleg niet begrijp, vraag ik een vraag.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik de uitleg niet begrijp, stel ik een vraag.
mistakes.why: 'Vraag' goes with 'stellen': een vraag stellen.

contrast.dutch: Ik stel een vraag omdat ik de uitleg niet begrijp.
contrast.english: I ask a question because I do not understand the explanation.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik stel'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The slow connection explains why the file went out later; both the cause and the effect are in the past.

clauses.subject: de verbinding
clauses.why: 'Traag' (slow) is the predicate and stands before the past verb 'was', which closes the clause.

clauses.text: heb ik het bestand later verstuurd
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the auxiliary 'heb' precedes 'ik'. The participle 'verstuurd' ends the main clause, behind the object and 'later'.

pat-omdat-35.meaning: You explain that you sent the file later, because the connection was slow.
pat-omdat-35.order: The background clause is in the simple past ('was'), the main clause in the perfect. After the front clause 'heb' comes first and the participle 'verstuurd' last. The verb pair wraps around the rest of the main clause: heb ... verstuurd.
pat-omdat-35.forms: versturen > verstuurd (perfect with hebben; the prefix ver- is inseparable, so no ge-). 'Het bestand' is a het-word. 'Later' = at a later time.
pat-omdat-35.compare: English 'I sent the file later' is a simple past. Dutch usually reports the event with the perfect 'heb verstuurd'. English 'the connection was slow' is the same simple past as Dutch.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de verbinding traag was, ik heb het bestand later verstuurd.
mistakes.right: Omdat de verbinding traag was, heb ik het bestand later verstuurd.
mistakes.why: The auxiliary 'heb' is the finite verb and must come second after the front clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de verbinding traag was, heb ik verstuurd het bestand later.
mistakes.right: Omdat de verbinding traag was, heb ik het bestand later verstuurd.
mistakes.why: The participle 'verstuurd' belongs at the end of the main clause.

contrast.dutch: Ik heb het bestand later verstuurd omdat de verbinding traag was.
contrast.english: I sent the file later because the connection was slow.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik heb ... verstuurd' wraps the object and adverb, and the reason clause follows.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The crowd on a past day is the reason for leaving early.

clauses.text: Omdat het gisteren zo druk was
clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: 'Gisteren zo druk' (so busy yesterday) comes before the past verb 'was', which ends the clause.

clauses.text: ben ik vroeg naar huis gegaan
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the auxiliary 'ben' precedes 'ik'. The participle 'gegaan' closes the clause; gaan takes zijn.

pat-omdat-36.meaning: You explain that you went home early yesterday, because it was so busy.
pat-omdat-36.order: The reason clause is a long block of adverbs and the predicate, ending with 'was'. The main clause is a perfect with zijn, so 'ben' comes second and 'gegaan' last, with 'vroeg naar huis' in between.
pat-omdat-36.forms: gaan > gegaan (perfect with zijn: a movement). 'Naar huis' = home (direction). 'Zo druk' = so busy. 'Het was druk' uses the empty subject 'het'.
pat-omdat-36.compare: English 'I went home early' is a simple past. Dutch tends to use 'ben ... gegaan'. English 'because it was so busy' keeps 'was' second; Dutch puts it last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het gisteren zo druk was, heb ik vroeg naar huis gegaan.
mistakes.right: Omdat het gisteren zo druk was, ben ik vroeg naar huis gegaan.
mistakes.why: Verbs of movement like gaan take zijn, not hebben.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het gisteren zo was druk, ben ik vroeg naar huis gegaan.
mistakes.right: Omdat het gisteren zo druk was, ben ik vroeg naar huis gegaan.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'was' goes behind the predicate 'druk'.

contrast.dutch: Ik ben vroeg naar huis gegaan omdat het gisteren zo druk was.
contrast.english: I went home early because it was so busy yesterday.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik ben ... gegaan' wraps around 'vroeg naar huis'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Having forgotten the keys is the earlier event that caused the call to the neighbour.

clauses.text: Omdat zij haar sleutels vergeten was
clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: 'Vergeten was' is the group: the participle 'vergeten' before the finite 'was'. Vergeten forms its perfect with zijn. The order 'vergeten was' is common; 'was vergeten' also exists.

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the past verb 'belde' precedes 'ze'. 'Haar buurman' is the person phoned.

pat-omdat-37.meaning: You explain that she phoned her neighbour, because she had forgotten her keys.
pat-omdat-37.order: The dependent clause shows the earlier event in the past perfect ('vergeten was', she had forgotten). It fills position one, so the main verb 'belde' comes second. The past perfect marks the keys as forgotten before the call.
pat-omdat-37.forms: vergeten > vergeten (participle) with zijn: zij was vergeten. bellen, past: ze belde (regular, -de). 'Haar' is the possessive her; 'ze' and 'zij' are the same pronoun, with and without stress.
pat-omdat-37.compare: English 'she had forgotten' uses 'had'; Dutch uses 'was' with the participle because vergeten takes zijn. English keeps 'had forgotten' together; the Dutch group 'vergeten was' ends the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij haar sleutels had vergeten, belde ze haar buurman.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij haar sleutels vergeten was, belde ze haar buurman.
mistakes.why: Vergeten forms its perfect tenses with zijn, so the auxiliary is 'was'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij haar sleutels vergeten was, ze belde haar buurman.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij haar sleutels vergeten was, belde ze haar buurman.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is position one, so the main verb comes second.

contrast.dutch: Ze belde haar buurman omdat zij haar sleutels vergeten was.
contrast.english: She called her neighbour because she had forgotten her keys.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ze belde', and the reason clause ends with the group 'vergeten was'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The outage is the reason you switched to offline work.

clauses.subject: het internet
clauses.why: 'Weg zijn' (to be gone, to be down): the adverb 'weg' stands before the past verb 'was', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the past verb 'werkten' precedes 'we'. 'Offline' says how.

pat-omdat-38.meaning: You say that you worked offline because the internet was down.
pat-omdat-38.order: A short reason in the simple past comes first. The inversion in the main clause, 'werkten we', is the same as in the present tense: the finite verb is second whatever its tense.
pat-omdat-38.forms: werken, past plural: werkten. zijn: was. 'Het internet' is a het-word. 'Weg zijn' means to be gone; for a service it means that it is unavailable.
pat-omdat-38.compare: English 'the internet was down' uses 'down'; Dutch says it was 'weg' (away). English 'we worked offline' is subject-first; Dutch inverts after the front clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het internet was weg, werkten we offline.
mistakes.right: Omdat het internet weg was, werkten we offline.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'was' goes behind 'weg'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het internet weg was, we werkten offline.
mistakes.right: Omdat het internet weg was, werkten we offline.
mistakes.why: The main verb must come second after a fronted dependent clause.

contrast.dutch: We werkten offline omdat het internet weg was.
contrast.english: We worked offline because the internet was down.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'We werkten' in normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Having no time is the reason you decline.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Geen tijd hebben' (to have no time): the negated noun 'geen tijd' stands before the finite verb 'heb', which ends the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kan' precedes 'ik'. The infinitive 'komen' closes the clause, behind 'niet'.

pat-omdat-39.meaning: You decline an invitation and give the reason first: you have no time.
pat-omdat-39.order: Both clauses contain a negation, and each uses a different one: 'geen' negates the noun 'tijd' in the first, 'niet' negates the verb group in the second. The modal 'kan' comes second after the fronted clause, and the infinitive ends the sentence.
pat-omdat-39.forms: hebben: ik heb. kunnen: ik kan. Geen replaces 'niet een' before a noun without article. 'Niet komen' negates the verb phrase.
pat-omdat-39.compare: English 'I do not have time, so I cannot come' uses 'do not' and 'cannot'. Dutch has 'geen tijd heb' and 'kan niet komen'. English cannot split 'cannot'; Dutch 'kan ... niet komen' puts 'niet' before the infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik niet tijd heb, kan ik niet komen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik geen tijd heb, kan ik niet komen.
mistakes.why: A noun without an article is negated with 'geen'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik geen tijd heb, ik kan niet komen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik geen tijd heb, kan ik niet komen.
mistakes.why: After the fronted dependent clause the modal comes second.

contrast.dutch: Ik kan niet komen omdat ik geen tijd heb.
contrast.english: I cannot come because I have no time.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik kan niet komen' keeps normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Her wish to learn Dutch is the motive for taking a course.

clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: 'Wil leren' is a modal group: the finite 'wil' plus the infinitive 'leren', after the object 'Nederlands'. They close the clause.

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'volgt' precedes 'ze'. 'Een cursus volgen' means to take a course.

pat-omdat-40.meaning: You say that she is taking a course, because she wants to learn Dutch.
pat-omdat-40.order: The reason clause ends with the group 'wil leren', the finite modal before its infinitive. The clause is position one, so the main verb 'volgt' comes next and then 'ze'.
pat-omdat-40.forms: willen: zij wil. leren: infinitive after a modal. volgen: ze volgt. 'Een cursus volgen' = to take a course. Cursus is a de-word.
pat-omdat-40.compare: English 'she wants to learn Dutch' uses 'to'; Dutch uses a modal and a bare infinitive without 'te'. English 'takes a course' uses 'take'; Dutch uses 'volgen' (follow).

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij wil Nederlands leren, volgt ze een cursus.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij Nederlands wil leren, volgt ze een cursus.
mistakes.why: The object 'Nederlands' stands in front of the modal group in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij Nederlands wil leren, neemt ze een cursus.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij Nederlands wil leren, volgt ze een cursus.
mistakes.why: The Dutch collocation is 'een cursus volgen', not 'nemen'.

contrast.dutch: Ze volgt een cursus omdat zij Nederlands wil leren.
contrast.english: She is taking a course because she wants to learn Dutch.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ze volgt'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: A bus that did not run is the cause of the change of transport, told as a past story.

clauses.subject: de bus
clauses.why: 'Niet' stands before the past verb 'kwam', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the past verb 'nam' precedes 'ik'. 'De trein' is the object.

pat-omdat-41.meaning: You tell what you did that morning: the bus never came, so you took the train.
pat-omdat-41.order: A two-clause story in the simple past. The dependent clause puts 'niet' before 'kwam'; the main clause starts with 'nam' because the clause in front fills position one.
pat-omdat-41.forms: komen, past: kwam. nemen, past: nam. Both are strong verbs with a vowel change. 'De bus' and 'de trein' are de-words.
pat-omdat-41.compare: English 'because the bus didn't come' needs 'didn't'; Dutch has just 'niet kwam'. English 'I took the train' keeps subject first; Dutch has 'nam ik' after the fronted reason.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de bus kwam niet, nam ik de trein.
mistakes.right: Omdat de bus niet kwam, nam ik de trein.
mistakes.why: 'Niet' stands before the finite verb in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de bus niet kwam, ik nam de trein.
mistakes.right: Omdat de bus niet kwam, nam ik de trein.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause makes the past main verb come second.

contrast.dutch: Ik nam de trein omdat de bus niet kwam.
contrast.english: I took the train because the bus did not come.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik nam'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The flat battery is the reason why the call cannot be made.

clauses.subject: mijn telefoon
clauses.why: 'Leeg' (flat, empty) stands before the finite verb 'is', which ends the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kan' precedes 'ik'. The pronoun 'je' and 'niet' stand before the infinitive 'bellen', which ends the clause.

pat-omdat-42.meaning: You explain that you cannot ring someone because your phone is flat.
pat-omdat-42.order: After the fronted reason the modal 'kan' comes second. In the rest of the main clause the object pronoun 'je' stands before 'niet', and the infinitive 'bellen' is last: kan ik je niet bellen.
pat-omdat-42.forms: kunnen: ik kan. bellen after a modal is a bare infinitive. 'Telefoon' is a de-word. Dutch says the phone is 'leeg' (empty) when the battery is flat.
pat-omdat-42.compare: English 'my phone is dead' uses 'dead'; Dutch uses 'leeg'. English 'I cannot call you' has 'cannot' as one word; Dutch splits 'kan' and 'niet' around the pronoun.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn telefoon leeg is, kan ik niet je bellen.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn telefoon leeg is, kan ik je niet bellen.
mistakes.why: An unstressed object pronoun stands before the negation 'niet'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn telefoon is leeg, kan ik je niet bellen.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn telefoon leeg is, kan ik je niet bellen.
mistakes.why: 'Mijn telefoon is leeg' is main-clause order; after omdat 'leeg' stands in front of 'is'.

contrast.dutch: Ik kan je niet bellen omdat mijn telefoon leeg is.
contrast.english: I cannot call you because my phone is flat.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik kan je niet bellen' is the normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Being new is the reason for giving him support.

clauses.subject: hij
