clauses.why: 'Nieuw' (new) is the predicate and stands before 'is', which closes the clause.

clauses.text: helpen we hem bij zijn eerste taak
clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'helpen' precedes 'we'. 'Bij zijn eerste taak' completes it: helpen bij (to help with).

pat-omdat-43.meaning: You say that the team supports the newcomer with his first task, because he is new.
pat-omdat-43.order: A one-word predicate in the dependent clause, then the inverted main clause: 'helpen we hem'. The pronoun 'hem' comes before the prepositional phrase 'bij zijn eerste taak'.
pat-omdat-43.forms: helpen: wij helpen. Helpen bij = to help with. 'Zijn eerste taak': the possessive 'zijn' and the ordinal 'eerste' before the de-word 'taak'. 'Hem' is the object form of 'hij'.
pat-omdat-43.compare: English 'help him with his first task' uses 'with'; Dutch uses 'bij'. English keeps 'we help' in order; Dutch inverts after the fronted clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat hij is nieuw, helpen we hem bij zijn eerste taak.
mistakes.right: Omdat hij nieuw is, helpen we hem bij zijn eerste taak.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the predicate 'nieuw' stands before 'is'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat hij nieuw is, helpen we hem met zijn eerste taak.
mistakes.right: Omdat hij nieuw is, helpen we hem bij zijn eerste taak.
mistakes.why: Dutch uses 'helpen bij' for the task you help with.

contrast.dutch: We helpen hem bij zijn eerste taak omdat hij nieuw is.
contrast.english: We help him with his first task because he is new.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'We helpen'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The delayed project is the cause of the extra meeting.

clauses.subject: het project
clauses.why: 'Vertraging hebben' puts 'vertraging' before the finite verb 'heeft', which ends the clause.

clauses.text: plannen we een extra vergadering in
clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'plannen' precedes 'we'. Inplannen (to schedule) is separable, so the particle 'in' closes the clause behind the object.

pat-omdat-44.meaning: You say that the team schedules an extra meeting because the project is behind.
pat-omdat-44.order: The dependent clause uses the fixed expression 'vertraging heeft' at its end. The main clause inverts to 'plannen we', and the particle 'in' stays at the end behind 'een extra vergadering'.
pat-omdat-44.forms: inplannen = in + plannen: wij plannen in, perfect: wij hebben ingepland. 'Het project' is a het-word. 'Een extra vergadering' has no -e on 'extra'.
pat-omdat-44.compare: English 'schedule' has no particle; Dutch 'inplannen' splits. English 'the project is delayed' uses a participle; Dutch says the project 'has delay'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het project vertraging heeft, inplannen we een extra vergadering.
mistakes.right: Omdat het project vertraging heeft, plannen we een extra vergadering in.
mistakes.why: The separable verb splits in a main clause: 'plannen' second, 'in' last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het project heeft vertraging, plannen we een extra vergadering in.
mistakes.right: Omdat het project vertraging heeft, plannen we een extra vergadering in.
mistakes.why: The finite verb goes behind its object in the dependent clause.

contrast.dutch: We plannen een extra vergadering in omdat het project vertraging heeft.
contrast.english: We are scheduling an extra meeting because the project is delayed.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'We plannen ... in'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Knowing the explanation is the reason why you are allowed to inform the team.

clauses.text: Omdat jij de beste uitleg kent
clauses.subject: jij
clauses.why: The object 'de beste uitleg' (the best explanation) stands before the finite verb 'kent', which closes the clause. With 'jij' the verb ends in -t.

clauses.subject: jij
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'mag' precedes 'jij'. The separable infinitive 'inlichten' stays joined at the end.

pat-omdat-45.meaning: You tell a colleague that, since he knows the best explanation, he may inform the team.
pat-omdat-45.order: The reason ends in 'kent'. The main clause inverts to 'mag jij', then the object 'het team', and the separable infinitive 'inlichten' stays joined at the end because it follows a modal.
pat-omdat-45.forms: kennen: jij kent. mogen: jij mag. inlichten = in + lichten: after a modal it stays joined; as a finite verb it would split ('ik licht het team in'). 'De beste' is the superlative of goed with -e.
pat-omdat-45.compare: English 'you may inform the team' keeps verbs in a row; Dutch does too, but the object goes between the modal and the infinitive. English cannot invert after 'Because you know...' but Dutch must.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat jij de beste uitleg kent, mag jij het team in lichten.
mistakes.right: Omdat jij de beste uitleg kent, mag jij het team inlichten.
mistakes.why: After a modal the separable verb stays in one piece.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat jij de beste uitleg kent, jij mag het team inlichten.
mistakes.right: Omdat jij de beste uitleg kent, mag jij het team inlichten.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is position one, so the modal comes second.

contrast.dutch: Jij mag het team inlichten omdat jij de beste uitleg kent.
contrast.english: You may inform the team because you know the best explanation.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Jij mag', with the infinitive at the end of the main clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The sleeping children are the reason you keep quiet.

clauses.subject: de kinderen
clauses.why: A short clause: the plural subject 'de kinderen' and the plural verb 'slapen', which is last.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'zijn' precedes 'we'. 'Stil' (quiet) is the predicate.

pat-omdat-46.meaning: You tell a guest that you keep quiet because the children are asleep.
pat-omdat-46.order: Both clauses are very short, so the pattern shows clearly: dependent clause with the verb at the end, then the main clause with the verb 'zijn' before its subject. The predicate 'stil' ends the sentence.
pat-omdat-46.forms: slapen: de kinderen slapen. zijn: wij zijn. 'Stil zijn' means to be quiet. 'Kinderen' is the plural of 'kind' (irregular plural).
pat-omdat-46.compare: English 'because the children are asleep' uses 'are asleep'; Dutch uses the verb 'slapen' directly. English 'we are quiet' is subject-first; Dutch inverts to 'zijn we stil'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat slapen de kinderen, zijn we stil.
mistakes.right: Omdat de kinderen slapen, zijn we stil.
mistakes.why: After omdat the subject comes first and the verb last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de kinderen slapen, we zijn stil.
mistakes.right: Omdat de kinderen slapen, zijn we stil.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is position one, so 'zijn' has to be second.

contrast.dutch: We zijn stil omdat de kinderen slapen.
contrast.english: We are quiet because the children are asleep.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'We zijn stil' keeps subject-first order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The incomplete data is the reason you cannot yet decide.

clauses.text: Omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet zijn
clauses.subject: de gegevens
clauses.why: 'Gegevens' is plural, so the verb is 'zijn'. 'Nog niet compleet' (not yet complete) stands before it, and 'zijn' closes the clause.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kunnen' precedes 'we'. The negated object 'geen conclusie' stands before the infinitive 'trekken', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-47.meaning: You say that no conclusion can be drawn yet, because the data is not complete.
pat-omdat-47.order: A longer reason clause that ends with 'zijn', then an inverted main clause with a modal and an infinitive at the end. 'Een conclusie trekken' is the fixed way to say 'draw a conclusion'.
pat-omdat-47.forms: zijn: de gegevens zijn (plural). kunnen: wij kunnen. 'Een conclusie trekken' = to draw a conclusion (trekken = pull). 'Geen conclusie' negates the noun.
pat-omdat-47.compare: English 'the data is not complete' treats 'data' as singular; Dutch 'gegevens' is plural and needs 'zijn'. English 'draw a conclusion' uses 'draw'; Dutch uses 'trekken' (pull).

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet is, kunnen we geen conclusie trekken.
mistakes.right: Omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet zijn, kunnen we geen conclusie trekken.
mistakes.why: 'Gegevens' is plural: the verb must be 'zijn'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet zijn, kunnen we geen conclusie maken.
mistakes.right: Omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet zijn, kunnen we geen conclusie trekken.
mistakes.why: The fixed expression is 'een conclusie trekken', not 'maken'.

contrast.dutch: We kunnen geen conclusie trekken omdat de gegevens nog niet compleet zijn.
contrast.english: We cannot draw a conclusion because the data is not yet complete.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'We kunnen'; the data clause closes the sentence.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The recent move explains why you need a new doctor.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: A perfect with zijn: the participle 'verhuisd' stands before the finite verb 'ben', which closes the clause. Verhuizen takes zijn.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'zoek' precedes 'ik'. 'Een nieuwe huisarts' is the object; the adjective takes -e before the de-word.

pat-omdat-48.meaning: You say that you are looking for a new GP because you have moved.
pat-omdat-48.order: The perfect group 'verhuisd ben' ends the reason clause. The clause fills position one, so the main verb 'zoek' comes next and then 'ik'. The object ends the sentence.
pat-omdat-48.forms: verhuizen > verhuisd, perfect with zijn: ik ben verhuisd. zoeken: ik zoek. 'Huisarts' is a de-word, so 'nieuwe' takes -e after 'een'.
pat-omdat-48.compare: English 'because I have moved' uses 'have'; Dutch uses 'ben' with the participle because verhuizen is a change of place. English 'looking for' needs 'for'; Dutch 'zoeken' takes the object directly.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik verhuisd heb, zoek ik een nieuwe huisarts.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik verhuisd ben, zoek ik een nieuwe huisarts.
mistakes.why: Verhuizen forms its perfect with zijn, not hebben.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik verhuisd ben, ik zoek een nieuwe huisarts.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik verhuisd ben, zoek ik een nieuwe huisarts.
mistakes.why: The main verb comes second after the fronted clause.

contrast.dutch: Ik zoek een nieuwe huisarts omdat ik verhuisd ben.
contrast.english: I am looking for a new GP because I have moved.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik zoek'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Frequent travel is the reason for owning a large suitcase: a general cause, not a single event.

clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: The adverb 'vaak' (often) stands before the finite verb 'reist', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'heeft' precedes 'ze'. 'Een grote koffer' is the object; the adjective takes -e before the de-word.

pat-omdat-49.meaning: You say that she owns a big suitcase because she travels a lot.
pat-omdat-49.order: The frequency adverb 'vaak' stands before the verb inside the dependent clause. The clause fills position one, so 'heeft' leads the main clause and 'ze' follows. The sentence has two forms of the pronoun, 'zij' and 'ze', for the same person.
pat-omdat-49.forms: reizen: zij reist. hebben: ze heeft. 'Een grote koffer': groot > grote (-e before a de-word after 'een'). 'Zij' is the stressed, 'ze' the unstressed form.
pat-omdat-49.compare: English 'she travels a lot' needs 'a lot'; Dutch 'vaak' is a single word. English keeps 'she has a big suitcase' in order; Dutch inverts after the fronted reason.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij reist vaak, heeft ze een grote koffer.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij vaak reist, heeft ze een grote koffer.
mistakes.why: 'Vaak' stands before the verb, which is last in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat zij vaak reist, heeft ze een groot koffer.
mistakes.right: Omdat zij vaak reist, heeft ze een grote koffer.
mistakes.why: Koffer is a de-word, so the adjective after 'een' needs -e.

contrast.dutch: Ze heeft een grote koffer omdat zij vaak reist.
contrast.english: She has a big suitcase because she travels a lot.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ze heeft'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Sunday explains why most shops are closed: a general fact given as the cause.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: 'Het is zondag' becomes 'omdat het zondag is': the predicate noun 'zondag' (Sunday) stands before the finite verb.

clauses.subject: de meeste winkels
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'zijn' precedes the subject, here a full noun phrase 'de meeste winkels'. 'Gesloten' (closed) is the predicate participle.

pat-omdat-50.meaning: You explain that most shops are closed because it is Sunday.
pat-omdat-50.order: Inversion works with a noun-phrase subject as well as with a pronoun: 'zijn de meeste winkels gesloten'. The finite verb stays second and the whole subject phrase follows it as a block.
pat-omdat-50.forms: zijn: de winkels zijn (plural). 'De meeste' = most (a superlative of veel). 'Gesloten' is the participle of sluiten used as a predicate.
pat-omdat-50.compare: English 'most shops are closed' keeps the subject before 'are'; Dutch puts 'zijn' first and the subject after it. English 'it is Sunday' does not move 'is'; Dutch puts 'is' last in the omdat clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het zondag is, de meeste winkels zijn gesloten.
mistakes.right: Omdat het zondag is, zijn de meeste winkels gesloten.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause fills position one, so the verb comes second, even before a long subject.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat het is zondag, zijn de meeste winkels gesloten.
mistakes.right: Omdat het zondag is, zijn de meeste winkels gesloten.
mistakes.why: After omdat the verb 'is' goes to the end.

contrast.dutch: De meeste winkels zijn gesloten omdat het zondag is.
contrast.english: Most shops are closed because it is Sunday.
contrast.note: Main clause first: the noun-phrase subject opens the sentence, so 'zijn' is simply second.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Not being finished is the reason you cannot help right now.

clauses.text: Omdat ik nog niet klaar ben
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Nog niet klaar' (not yet finished) stands before the finite verb 'ben', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kan' precedes 'ik'. 'Je' and 'niet' come before the infinitive 'helpen', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-51.meaning: You tell a colleague you cannot help yet, because you are still busy with your own task.
pat-omdat-51.order: A reason with 'nog niet klaar ben' and a main clause with a modal and an infinitive. The two negations are separate: the first negates the state of being finished, the second the possibility of helping.
pat-omdat-51.forms: klaar zijn: ik ben klaar. kunnen: ik kan. 'Nog niet' = not yet. 'Je' is the unstressed object, placed before 'niet'.
pat-omdat-51.compare: English 'I am not finished yet, so I cannot help you' needs two sentences or a conjunction; Dutch packs the reason in front and uses the modal 'kan' second.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik nog niet klaar ben, ik kan je niet helpen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik nog niet klaar ben, kan ik je niet helpen.
mistakes.why: A modal verb must be second after a fronted dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik niet nog klaar ben, kan ik je niet helpen.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik nog niet klaar ben, kan ik je niet helpen.
mistakes.why: 'Nog' goes in front of 'niet' in the fixed phrase 'nog niet' (not yet).

contrast.dutch: Ik kan je niet helpen omdat ik nog niet klaar ben.
contrast.english: I cannot help you because I am not finished yet.
contrast.note: Main clause first: 'Ik kan je niet helpen' keeps normal order.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Their lateness is the reason you did not wait.

clauses.subject: jullie
clauses.why: 'Te laat' (too late) stands before the finite verb 'zijn', which closes the clause. 'Jullie' is the plural 'you'.

clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'beginnen' precedes 'we'. 'Zonder jullie' (without you) completes it.

pat-omdat-52.meaning: You tell latecomers that you started without them, because they were late.
pat-omdat-52.order: The reason clause ends with 'zijn'. The main clause starts with 'beginnen', since the clause in front is position one. 'Zonder jullie' ends the sentence.
pat-omdat-52.forms: zijn: jullie zijn. beginnen: wij beginnen. 'Te laat zijn' = to be late. 'Zonder' (without) is followed by 'jullie', the same form as the subject.
pat-omdat-52.compare: English 'because you are late' keeps 'are' second; Dutch ends with 'zijn'. English 'we are starting without you' keeps subject first; Dutch has 'beginnen we'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat jullie zijn te laat, beginnen we zonder jullie.
mistakes.right: Omdat jullie te laat zijn, beginnen we zonder jullie.
mistakes.why: The finite verb goes behind 'te laat' after omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat jullie te laat zijn, we beginnen zonder jullie.
mistakes.right: Omdat jullie te laat zijn, beginnen we zonder jullie.
mistakes.why: The fronted clause is position one; the main verb is second.

contrast.dutch: We beginnen zonder jullie omdat jullie te laat zijn.
contrast.english: We are starting without you because you are late.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'We beginnen'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The forgotten password is the cause of the new link.

clauses.text: Omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord vergeten is
clauses.subject: de gebruiker
clauses.why: 'Vergeten is' (the participle before the finite 'is') closes the clause behind the object 'het wachtwoord'. Vergeten takes zijn.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'stuur' precedes 'ik'. 'Een nieuwe link' is the object.

pat-omdat-53.meaning: You say that you send a new link because the user has forgotten the password.
pat-omdat-53.order: The reason ends with the group 'vergeten is', behind the object. The main clause then inverts to 'stuur ik'. The object 'een nieuwe link' ends the sentence, with 'nieuwe' carrying -e before the de-word.
pat-omdat-53.forms: vergeten > vergeten (perfect with zijn: de gebruiker is vergeten). sturen: ik stuur. 'Wachtwoord' is a het-word. 'Link' is a de-word.
pat-omdat-53.compare: English 'the user has forgotten' uses 'has'; Dutch uses 'is' because vergeten takes zijn. English 'send a new link' follows the same order as Dutch.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord heeft vergeten, stuur ik een nieuwe link.
mistakes.right: Omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord vergeten is, stuur ik een nieuwe link.
mistakes.why: Vergeten forms its perfect with zijn, so the auxiliary is 'is'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord vergeten is, ik stuur een nieuwe link.
mistakes.right: Omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord vergeten is, stuur ik een nieuwe link.
mistakes.why: The finite verb comes second after the fronted dependent clause.

contrast.dutch: Ik stuur een nieuwe link omdat de gebruiker het wachtwoord vergeten is.
contrast.english: I am sending a new link because the user has forgotten the password.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik stuur'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: A birthday is the occasion that makes you phone your father.

clauses.subject: mijn vader
clauses.why: 'Jarig' (having a birthday) stands before the finite verb 'is', which closes the clause.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'bel' precedes 'ik'. Opbellen (to phone) is separable, so the particle 'op' closes the clause after 'hem vanavond'.

pat-omdat-54.meaning: You say that you will phone your father tonight, because it is his birthday.
pat-omdat-54.order: The reason uses the Dutch word 'jarig zijn' (to have one's birthday). After it the main clause inverts to 'bel ik', and the separable particle 'op' ends the clause, behind 'hem vanavond'.
pat-omdat-54.forms: opbellen = op + bellen: ik bel op (common in Belgian Dutch; 'bellen' alone is also used). 'Jarig zijn' is an adjective; 'de verjaardag' is the noun. 'Vanavond' = this evening.
pat-omdat-54.compare: English 'it is my father's birthday' uses a noun; Dutch has the adjective 'jarig'. English 'call him up' has a particle after the pronoun; Dutch puts 'op' at the very end.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn vader jarig is, opbel ik hem vanavond.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn vader jarig is, bel ik hem vanavond op.
mistakes.why: In a main clause the separable verb splits and the particle goes last.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat mijn vader is jarig, bel ik hem vanavond op.
mistakes.right: Omdat mijn vader jarig is, bel ik hem vanavond op.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes behind 'jarig'.

contrast.dutch: Ik bel hem vanavond op omdat mijn vader jarig is.
contrast.english: I am calling him tonight because it is my father's birthday.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik bel ... op'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The closed road is the reason for choosing the train.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'neem' is simply second; 'de trein' is the object.

clauses.subject: de weg
clauses.why: 'Afgesloten is' is the group: the participle of afsluiten stands before the finite 'is' and closes the clause.

pat-omdat-55.meaning: You say that you take the train because the road is closed.
pat-omdat-55.order: A plain main clause is followed by a dependent clause that ends in 'afgesloten is'. The participle works as a state here (the road is closed), so 'is' is a form of zijn, not the perfect auxiliary of an action.
pat-omdat-55.forms: afsluiten > afgesloten (separable participle: af + ge + sloten). 'De weg is afgesloten' describes the state. nemen: ik neem.
pat-omdat-55.compare: English 'the road is closed' is the same pattern. In Dutch the participle comes before 'is' in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik neem de trein omdat is de weg afgesloten.
mistakes.right: Ik neem de trein omdat de weg afgesloten is.
mistakes.why: After omdat the subject comes first; verb-before-subject belongs to main clauses, not to the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik neem de trein omdat de weg afsluiten is.
mistakes.right: Ik neem de trein omdat de weg afgesloten is.
mistakes.why: A state needs the participle 'afgesloten', not the infinitive.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de weg afgesloten is, neem ik de trein.
contrast.english: Because the road is closed, I am taking the train.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'neem ik de trein'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The flu is the cause of the absence, stated in the second half.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so 'komt' is second. 'Niet' follows the verb and negates the whole statement.

clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: 'Griep hebben' (to have the flu): the noun 'griep' stands before the finite verb 'heeft', which ends the sentence.

pat-omdat-56.meaning: You say that he is not coming, because he has the flu.
pat-omdat-56.order: A negative main clause, then the dependent clause ending in 'heeft'. 'Griep' has no article, since Dutch treats illnesses with 'hebben' without an article.
pat-omdat-56.forms: komen: hij komt. hebben: hij heeft. 'Griep hebben' = to have the flu; the noun takes no article.
pat-omdat-56.compare: English 'he has the flu' needs 'the'; Dutch 'griep heeft' has no article. English 'because he has' keeps 'has' before 'the flu'; Dutch ends with 'heeft'.

mistakes.wrong: Hij komt niet omdat hij heeft griep.
mistakes.right: Hij komt niet omdat hij griep heeft.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the finite verb goes behind its object.

mistakes.wrong: Hij komt niet omdat hij de griep heeft.
mistakes.right: Hij komt niet omdat hij griep heeft.
mistakes.why: 'Griep' is used without an article in this expression.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij griep heeft, komt hij niet.
contrast.english: Because he has the flu, he is not coming.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'komt hij niet'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The start of maintenance is the reason for the shutdown.

clauses.subject: Wij
clauses.why: Afsluiten is separable: 'sluiten ... af' splits around the object 'de computer'.

clauses.subject: het onderhoud
clauses.why: The subject 'het onderhoud' is followed directly by the finite verb 'begint', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-57.meaning: You say that you shut the computer down because maintenance is starting.
pat-omdat-57.order: The separable verb splits in the main clause: sluiten ... af. The dependent clause has no object, so the verb follows the subject directly, and the sentence ends with 'begint'.
pat-omdat-57.forms: afsluiten = af + sluiten: wij sluiten af, perfect: wij hebben afgesloten. 'Onderhoud' is a het-word. beginnen: het begint.
pat-omdat-57.compare: English 'shut down' has the particle after the verb or object; Dutch has it last. English 'maintenance is starting' keeps the verb after the subject; Dutch also does, but only because the clause has no other words.

mistakes.wrong: Wij afsluiten de computer omdat het onderhoud begint.
mistakes.right: Wij sluiten de computer af omdat het onderhoud begint.
mistakes.why: In a main clause the separable verb splits: 'sluiten' second, 'af' last.

mistakes.wrong: Wij sluiten de computer af omdat begint het onderhoud.
mistakes.right: Wij sluiten de computer af omdat het onderhoud begint.
mistakes.why: The subject comes first and the verb last after omdat.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het onderhoud begint, sluiten wij de computer af.
contrast.english: Because maintenance is starting, we are shutting the computer down.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'sluiten wij ... af'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The wish to earn more explains the job change.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'heeft' is second. 'Een nieuwe baan' is the object, with -e on the adjective before the de-word.

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: 'Meer' (more) stands before the modal group 'wil verdienen', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-58.meaning: You say that she has a new job because she wants to earn more money.
pat-omdat-58.order: The main clause is simple. The dependent clause ends with the modal group 'wil verdienen', so the finite verb 'wil' is not the last word: the infinitive 'verdienen' is.
pat-omdat-58.forms: willen: ze wil (no ending). verdienen: infinitive after a modal. 'Meer' = more. 'Baan' is a de-word.
pat-omdat-58.compare: English 'she wants to earn more' uses 'to'; Dutch uses the bare infinitive after the modal. English keeps 'wants to earn' after the subject; Dutch moves the pair to the end.

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft een nieuwe baan omdat ze wil meer verdienen.
mistakes.right: Zij heeft een nieuwe baan omdat ze meer wil verdienen.
mistakes.why: 'Meer' comes before the modal group in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Zij heeft een nieuwe baan omdat ze meer wil te verdienen.
mistakes.right: Zij heeft een nieuwe baan omdat ze meer wil verdienen.
mistakes.why: A modal takes a bare infinitive; 'te' is not used.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ze meer wil verdienen, heeft zij een nieuwe baan.
contrast.english: Because she wants to earn more, she has a new job.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'heeft zij'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The missing data blocks the start; the reason follows the main statement.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: The modal 'kunnen' is second; the infinitive 'beginnen' closes the clause, behind 'niet'.

clauses.subject: de gegevens
clauses.why: 'Gegevens' is plural, so the verb 'ontbreken' (to be missing) is plural, too, and it closes the clause.

pat-omdat-59.meaning: You say that you cannot start because the data is missing.
pat-omdat-59.order: A main clause with a modal and infinitive is followed by a dependent clause containing only the subject and a verb. The pattern 'omdat + subject + verb' is the minimal omdat clause.
pat-omdat-59.forms: ontbreken: de gegevens ontbreken (plural). kunnen: wij kunnen. 'Ontbreken' is inseparable: ont- is a fixed prefix, so the verb never splits.
pat-omdat-59.compare: English 'the data is missing' treats data as singular; Dutch 'gegevens' is plural. English uses 'missing' as an adjective; Dutch has a verb.

mistakes.wrong: We kunnen niet beginnen omdat de gegevens ontbreekt.
mistakes.right: We kunnen niet beginnen omdat de gegevens ontbreken.
mistakes.why: 'Gegevens' is plural, so the verb needs -en.

mistakes.wrong: We kunnen niet beginnen omdat ontbreken de gegevens.
mistakes.right: We kunnen niet beginnen omdat de gegevens ontbreken.
mistakes.why: The subject comes first after omdat; the verb comes last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de gegevens ontbreken, kunnen we niet beginnen.
contrast.english: Because the data is missing, we cannot start.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'kunnen we niet beginnen'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: An unsolved problem is the reason you ask your manager for help.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'bel' is second; 'mijn manager' is the object.

clauses.text: omdat ik een probleem niet kan oplossen
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The object 'een probleem' and 'niet' stand before the modal group 'kan oplossen', which closes the clause. 'Oplossen' is a joined infinitive after the modal.

pat-omdat-60.meaning: You say that you are phoning your manager, because you cannot solve a problem yourself.
pat-omdat-60.order: The dependent clause lines up the object, the negation, and the modal group: een probleem niet kan oplossen. The infinitive 'oplossen' is last. In a main clause with a modal the infinitive would also be last, but the pieces before it would follow the modal directly.
pat-omdat-60.forms: oplossen = op + lossen. After a modal it is joined. kunnen: ik kan. 'Een probleem oplossen' = to solve a problem. 'Niet' stands before the verb group.
pat-omdat-60.compare: English 'I cannot solve a problem' has 'cannot' together; Dutch splits 'niet' and 'kan' and puts the object and 'niet' before the modal in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel mijn manager omdat ik kan niet een probleem oplossen.
mistakes.right: Ik bel mijn manager omdat ik een probleem niet kan oplossen.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause 'niet' and the object stand before the modal group.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel mijn manager omdat ik een probleem niet kan lossen op.
mistakes.right: Ik bel mijn manager omdat ik een probleem niet kan oplossen.
mistakes.why: After a modal the separable infinitive stays in one piece.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik een probleem niet kan oplossen, bel ik mijn manager.
contrast.english: Because I cannot solve a problem, I am phoning my manager.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'bel ik mijn manager'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The director's illness is the reason the meeting was moved.

clauses.subject: De vergadering
clauses.why: The subject comes first, so 'is' is second. 'Uitgesteld' (postponed) is a participle closing the main clause.

clauses.subject: de directeur
clauses.why: 'Ziek' stands before the finite verb 'is', which closes the sentence.

pat-omdat-61.meaning: You report that the meeting has been postponed, because the director is ill.
pat-omdat-61.order: The main clause is a passive-like state with 'is uitgesteld'. The two forms of 'is' sit in different positions: second in the main clause, last in the dependent clause. This is a quick visual test of the two orders.
pat-omdat-61.forms: uitstellen > uitgesteld (separable participle: uit + ge + steld). 'Is uitgesteld' says the postponement has happened. zijn: de directeur is.
pat-omdat-61.compare: English 'has been postponed' uses 'has been'; Dutch simply says 'is uitgesteld'. English 'because the director is ill' keeps 'is' next to the subject; Dutch moves it to the end.

mistakes.wrong: De vergadering is uitgesteld omdat de directeur is ziek.
mistakes.right: De vergadering is uitgesteld omdat de directeur ziek is.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause 'ziek' has to stand before 'is': after omdat the clause reads de directeur ziek is.

mistakes.wrong: De vergadering uitgesteld is omdat de directeur ziek is.
mistakes.right: De vergadering is uitgesteld omdat de directeur ziek is.
mistakes.why: In the main clause the finite verb 'is' must be second; the participle goes to the end.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de directeur ziek is, is de vergadering uitgesteld.
contrast.english: Because the director is ill, the meeting has been postponed.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main verb inverts, so the two 'is' forms now stand close together across the comma.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The train's early departure is the reason for getting up early.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Opstaan (to get up) is separable: 'sta ... op'. The adverb 'vroeg' stands between the verb and the particle.

clauses.text: omdat de eerste trein om zes uur vertrekt
clauses.subject: de eerste trein
clauses.why: The time phrase 'om zes uur' stands before the finite verb 'vertrekt', which closes the clause. 'Vertrekken' is inseparable.

pat-omdat-62.meaning: You say that you get up early, because the first train leaves at six.
pat-omdat-62.order: The main clause splits opstaan around 'vroeg'. The dependent clause puts the time phrase before 'vertrekt', so the sentence ends with the verb. The subject 'de eerste trein' includes an ordinal number.
pat-omdat-62.forms: opstaan = op + staan: ik sta op, perfect: ik ben opgestaan (with zijn). vertrekken: de trein vertrekt. 'De eerste' = the first; 'om zes uur' = at six o'clock.
pat-omdat-62.compare: English 'get up' keeps 'up' next to 'get'; Dutch has 'sta ... op'. English 'leaves at six' keeps 'leaves' before 'at six'; Dutch puts 'vertrekt' last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik sta vroeg op omdat de eerste trein vertrekt om zes uur.
mistakes.right: Ik sta vroeg op omdat de eerste trein om zes uur vertrekt.
mistakes.why: The time phrase belongs in front of the final verb in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik opsta vroeg omdat de eerste trein om zes uur vertrekt.
mistakes.right: Ik sta vroeg op omdat de eerste trein om zes uur vertrekt.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'sta' second, 'op' last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de eerste trein om zes uur vertrekt, sta ik vroeg op.
contrast.english: Because the first train leaves at six, I get up early.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'sta ik vroeg op'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Feeling unwell in the past explains the departure.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: A perfect with zijn: 'is' is second and the participle 'gegaan' closes the main clause, after 'naar huis'.

clauses.text: omdat hij zich niet goed voelde
clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: The reflexive 'zich' and 'niet goed' stand before the past verb 'voelde', which closes the clause. 'Zich voelen' is reflexive.

pat-omdat-63.meaning: You report that he went home because he did not feel well.
pat-omdat-63.order: The perfect wraps the direction: is ... gegaan. In the dependent clause the reflexive pronoun comes right after the subject, then 'niet goed', and the past verb 'voelde' ends the sentence.
pat-omdat-63.forms: gaan > gegaan with zijn. zich voelen: hij voelde zich (reflexive). 'Zich' is the reflexive pronoun for hij/zij/het. 'Niet goed' = not well.
pat-omdat-63.compare: English 'he did not feel well' uses do-support and no reflexive. Dutch uses the reflexive verb 'zich voelen' with 'niet goed' before the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Hij is naar huis gegaan omdat hij voelde zich niet goed.
mistakes.right: Hij is naar huis gegaan omdat hij zich niet goed voelde.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the reflexive and adverbs come first and the verb last.

mistakes.wrong: Hij is naar huis gegaan omdat hij hem niet goed voelde.
mistakes.right: Hij is naar huis gegaan omdat hij zich niet goed voelde.
mistakes.why: With the same subject the reflexive pronoun is 'zich', not 'hem'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij zich niet goed voelde, is hij naar huis gegaan.
contrast.english: Because he did not feel well, he went home.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'is hij ... gegaan'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Forgetting quickly is the cause of the writing habit.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Opschrijven is separable: 'schrijf ... op' around the object 'alles'.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The adverb 'snel' stands before the finite verb 'vergeet', which closes the clause. 'Vergeten' is used without an object here.

pat-omdat-64.meaning: You say that you write everything down because you forget quickly.
pat-omdat-64.order: Both clauses are short. The main clause splits the separable verb around 'alles', and the dependent clause ends with 'vergeet' behind 'snel'.
pat-omdat-64.forms: opschrijven: ik schrijf op. vergeten: ik vergeet (the e is long, written 'ee' in a closed syllable). 'Alles' = everything.
pat-omdat-64.compare: English 'write down' has 'down' after the verb or object; Dutch has 'op' last. English 'forget quickly' keeps 'forget' first; Dutch puts the verb last in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik schrijf alles op omdat ik vergeet snel.
mistakes.right: Ik schrijf alles op omdat ik snel vergeet.
mistakes.why: The adverb 'snel' stands before the final verb.

mistakes.wrong: Ik schrijf op alles omdat ik snel vergeet.
mistakes.right: Ik schrijf alles op omdat ik snel vergeet.
mistakes.why: The particle 'op' goes after the object, at the end of the main clause.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik snel vergeet, schrijf ik alles op.
contrast.english: Because I forget quickly, I write everything down.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'schrijf ik alles op'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The cold room is the cause of switching on the heating.

clauses.subject: Ze
clauses.why: Aanzetten (to switch on) is separable: 'zet ... aan' around the object 'de verwarming'.

clauses.text: omdat het in de kamer koud is
clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: The place phrase 'in de kamer' and the predicate 'koud' stand before the finite verb 'is', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-65.meaning: You say that she turns the heating on because it is cold in the room.
pat-omdat-65.order: In the dependent clause the place phrase comes before the predicate, so 'koud is' stays together at the end. The main clause splits aanzetten around the object.
pat-omdat-65.forms: aanzetten: ze zet aan, perfect: ze heeft aangezet. 'Verwarming' is a de-word. 'In de kamer' says where it is cold.
pat-omdat-65.compare: English 'it is cold in the room' keeps 'is' before 'cold'. Dutch moves it behind 'koud'. English 'turns on the heating' can put the particle before the object; Dutch puts it at the end of the main clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ze zet de verwarming aan omdat het is koud in de kamer.
mistakes.right: Ze zet de verwarming aan omdat het in de kamer koud is.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the predicate and the place come before the finite verb.

mistakes.wrong: Ze aanzet de verwarming omdat het in de kamer koud is.
mistakes.right: Ze zet de verwarming aan omdat het in de kamer koud is.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'zet' second, 'aan' last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat het in de kamer koud is, zet ze de verwarming aan.
contrast.english: Because it is cold in the room, she turns the heating on.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'zet ze ... aan'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The customer's absence is the reason the appointment was changed; both are past events.

clauses.subject: Wij
clauses.why: A perfect: 'hebben' is second and the participle 'verplaatst' closes the main clause, after the object.

clauses.text: omdat de klant niet kon komen
clauses.subject: de klant
clauses.why: 'Niet kon komen' is a past modal group: the finite 'kon' plus the infinitive 'komen', behind 'niet'. 'Kon' is not the last word.

pat-omdat-66.meaning: You report that you moved the appointment because the customer could not come.
pat-omdat-66.order: The main clause uses the perfect, so the auxiliary and participle wrap the object. The dependent clause uses a past modal and an infinitive: the pair 'kon komen' closes the clause behind 'niet'.
pat-omdat-66.forms: verplaatsen > verplaatst (perfect with hebben; inseparable prefix ver-). kunnen, past: kon. 'Niet kon komen' = could not come.
pat-omdat-66.compare: English 'could not come' keeps the verbs together after the subject; Dutch puts 'niet' first and the pair 'kon komen' at the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Wij hebben de afspraak verplaatst omdat de klant kon niet komen.
mistakes.right: Wij hebben de afspraak verplaatst omdat de klant niet kon komen.
mistakes.why: After omdat 'niet' stands before the verb group.

mistakes.wrong: Wij hebben verplaatst de afspraak omdat de klant niet kon komen.
mistakes.right: Wij hebben de afspraak verplaatst omdat de klant niet kon komen.
mistakes.why: With the perfect, the participle 'verplaatst' belongs at the end of the main clause, after the object 'de afspraak'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de klant niet kon komen, hebben wij de afspraak verplaatst.
contrast.english: Because the customer could not come, we moved the appointment.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'hebben wij', with the participle still last.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The planned update is the reason for the safety copy: a reason that points to the future.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'maak' is second; 'een back-up' is the object.

clauses.text: omdat ik de update morgen wil installeren
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The object 'de update' and 'morgen' stand before the modal group 'wil installeren', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-67.meaning: You explain that you make a backup because you want to install the update tomorrow.
pat-omdat-67.order: A plain main clause is followed by a dependent clause where the object and time phrase precede the group 'wil installeren'. 'Morgen' is inside the dependent clause, so it dates the update and not the backup.
pat-omdat-67.forms: maken: ik maak. willen: ik wil. installeren is an infinitive after the modal. 'De update' is a de-word; 'back-up' is written with a hyphen.
pat-omdat-67.compare: English 'I want to install the update tomorrow' keeps 'want to install' together. Dutch ends the clause with the pair 'wil installeren'. English needs 'to'; Dutch uses the bare infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: Ik maak een back-up omdat ik wil de update morgen installeren.
mistakes.right: Ik maak een back-up omdat ik de update morgen wil installeren.
mistakes.why: After omdat the modal group goes to the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik maak een back-up omdat ik de update morgen wil te installeren.
mistakes.right: Ik maak een back-up omdat ik de update morgen wil installeren.
mistakes.why: A modal takes a bare infinitive, without 'te'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik de update morgen wil installeren, maak ik een back-up.
contrast.english: Because I want to install the update tomorrow, I am making a backup.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'maak ik een back-up'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The late delivery is the cause of the customer's anger.

clauses.subject: De klant
clauses.why: The subject comes first, so 'is' is second; 'boos' (angry) is the predicate.

clauses.text: omdat zijn bestelling te laat is aangekomen
clauses.subject: zijn bestelling
clauses.why: The perfect group 'is aangekomen' (zijn plus the joined participle of aankomen) closes the clause behind 'te laat'. Aankomen takes zijn.

pat-omdat-68.meaning: You explain that the customer is angry, because his order arrived too late.
pat-omdat-68.order: The main clause is a short statement of a state. The dependent clause reports a past event with a perfect group, 'is aangekomen', at its end. The finite 'is' is therefore not the last word.
pat-omdat-68.forms: aankomen > aangekomen (zijn; separable participle aan + ge + komen). 'Te laat' = too late. 'Zijn bestelling': possessive 'zijn' (his) plus a de-word.
pat-omdat-68.compare: English 'his order arrived too late' uses a simple past. Dutch tends to say 'is aangekomen' (has arrived). English 'too late' is the same as 'te laat'.

mistakes.wrong: De klant is boos omdat zijn bestelling heeft aangekomen te laat.
mistakes.right: De klant is boos omdat zijn bestelling te laat is aangekomen.
mistakes.why: Aankomen takes zijn, and 'te laat' comes before the verb group.

mistakes.wrong: De klant is boos omdat zijn bestelling is te laat aangekomen.
mistakes.right: De klant is boos omdat zijn bestelling te laat is aangekomen.
mistakes.why: The adverb phrase 'te laat' stands before the auxiliary in this order.

contrast.dutch: Omdat zijn bestelling te laat is aangekomen, is de klant boos.
contrast.english: Because his order arrived too late, the customer is angry.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'is de klant boos'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The heavy box is the reason you offer help.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'help' is second; 'mijn buurman' is the person helped.

clauses.text: omdat hij een zware doos moet dragen
clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: The object 'een zware doos' stands before the modal group 'moet dragen', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-69.meaning: You say that you help your neighbour because he has to carry a heavy box.
pat-omdat-69.order: A simple main clause is followed by a dependent clause that ends with a modal and an infinitive. The adjective 'zware' takes -e before the de-word 'doos'.
pat-omdat-69.forms: helpen: ik help (no ending). moeten: hij moet. dragen: infinitive after the modal. 'Een zware doos': zwaar > zware before a de-word with 'een'.
pat-omdat-69.compare: English 'he has to carry' uses 'has to'. Dutch uses the modal 'moet'. English keeps 'has to carry a heavy box' in order; Dutch puts the object first and the verbs last.

mistakes.wrong: Ik help mijn buurman omdat hij moet dragen een zware doos.
mistakes.right: Ik help mijn buurman omdat hij een zware doos moet dragen.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the object comes before the modal group.

mistakes.wrong: Ik help mijn buurman omdat hij een zwaar doos moet dragen.
mistakes.right: Ik help mijn buurman omdat hij een zware doos moet dragen.
mistakes.why: Doos is a de-word, so the adjective after 'een' takes -e.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij een zware doos moet dragen, help ik mijn buurman.
contrast.english: Because he has to carry a heavy box, I am helping my neighbour.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'help ik mijn buurman'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Being the responsible person is the ground for the permission to decide.

clauses.subject: Jij
clauses.why: The modal 'mag' is second; the infinitive 'nemen' closes the main clause, behind the object.

clauses.subject: jij
clauses.why: The predicate 'de verantwoordelijke' (the responsible person) stands before the finite verb 'bent', which closes the sentence.

pat-omdat-70.meaning: You tell a colleague that he may take the decision, because he is the one responsible.
pat-omdat-70.order: The main clause has a modal and an infinitive with the object between them. The dependent clause has a predicate noun phrase before 'bent', and the sentence ends with the verb.
pat-omdat-70.forms: mogen: jij mag. nemen: infinitive. 'Een beslissing nemen' = to take a decision. zijn: jij bent. 'De verantwoordelijke' is an adjective used as a noun.
pat-omdat-70.compare: English 'you may take the decision' also uses a modal. English 'you are the one responsible' keeps 'are' second; Dutch ends with 'bent'.

mistakes.wrong: Jij mag de beslissing nemen omdat jij bent de verantwoordelijke.
mistakes.right: Jij mag de beslissing nemen omdat jij de verantwoordelijke bent.
mistakes.why: Behind omdat the predicate noun phrase 'de verantwoordelijke' stands before 'bent', not after it.

mistakes.wrong: Jij mag de beslissing maken omdat jij de verantwoordelijke bent.
mistakes.right: Jij mag de beslissing nemen omdat jij de verantwoordelijke bent.
mistakes.why: Dutch says 'een beslissing nemen', not 'maken'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat jij de verantwoordelijke bent, mag jij de beslissing nemen.
contrast.english: Because you are the one responsible, you may take the decision.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'mag jij'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The blocked access is the reason for contacting the administrator.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so 'bellen' is second; 'de beheerder' is the object.

clauses.subject: de toegang
clauses.why: 'Geblokkeerd' (blocked) is a participle used as a predicate before the finite verb 'is', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-71.meaning: You say that you are phoning the administrator, because access is blocked.
pat-omdat-71.order: The main clause is short. The dependent clause ends with 'geblokkeerd is', the participle before the finite verb. The state 'blocked' is described, not an action by someone.
pat-omdat-71.forms: blokkeren > geblokkeerd. bellen: wij bellen. 'De toegang' (access) is a de-word. 'Beheerder' = administrator.
pat-omdat-71.compare: English 'access is blocked' keeps 'is' second; Dutch ends with it. English uses 'call' with the object directly, as Dutch does here.

mistakes.wrong: We bellen de beheerder omdat is de toegang geblokkeerd.
mistakes.right: We bellen de beheerder omdat de toegang geblokkeerd is.
mistakes.why: After omdat the subject comes first; putting the verb before the subject belongs to main clauses only.

mistakes.wrong: We bellen de beheerder omdat de toegang geblokkeerd.
mistakes.right: We bellen de beheerder omdat de toegang geblokkeerd is.
mistakes.why: The participle needs the finite verb 'is' in the clause.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de toegang geblokkeerd is, bellen we de beheerder.
contrast.english: Because access is blocked, we are phoning the administrator.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'bellen we de beheerder'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The obligation to work tomorrow is the reason you decline.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Meegaan (to come along) is separable: 'ga ... mee'. 'Niet' stands before the particle.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Morgen' stands before the modal group 'moet werken', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-72.meaning: You decline an outing, because you must work tomorrow.
pat-omdat-72.order: The main clause splits meegaan around 'niet', so the particle 'mee' is last. The dependent clause puts the time phrase before the modal group 'moet werken'.
pat-omdat-72.forms: meegaan = mee + gaan: ik ga mee, perfect: ik ben meegegaan. moeten: ik moet. 'Moeten' (must) is the way to say 'have to'.
pat-omdat-72.compare: English 'I am not coming along' has 'along' after the verb; Dutch has 'mee' at the end. English 'I have to work' uses 'have to'; Dutch uses the modal 'moet'.

mistakes.wrong: Ik ga niet mee omdat ik moet werken morgen.
mistakes.right: Ik ga niet mee omdat ik morgen moet werken.
mistakes.why: The time phrase goes before the modal group in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik meega niet omdat ik morgen moet werken.
mistakes.right: Ik ga niet mee omdat ik morgen moet werken.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'ga' second, 'mee' last.

contrast.dutch: Omdat ik morgen moet werken, ga ik niet mee.
contrast.english: Because I have to work tomorrow, I am not coming along.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'ga ik niet mee'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Her husband's origin is the motive for learning French.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'leert' is second; 'Frans' is the object.

clauses.text: omdat haar man uit Wallonië komt
clauses.subject: haar man
clauses.why: The origin phrase 'uit Wallonië' stands before the finite verb 'komt', which closes the clause. 'Haar man' is her husband.

pat-omdat-73.meaning: You say that she is learning French because her husband comes from Wallonia.
pat-omdat-73.order: A simple main clause is followed by a dependent clause where 'uit Wallonië' precedes 'komt'. The verb 'komen' with 'uit' expresses origin.
pat-omdat-73.forms: leren: zij leert. komen uit = to come from. 'Frans' (the language) has no article. 'Haar man' = her husband (man also means man).
pat-omdat-73.compare: English 'comes from Wallonia' keeps 'comes' before 'from'; Dutch puts 'komt' last. English needs 'from'; Dutch uses 'uit'.

mistakes.wrong: Zij leert Frans omdat haar man komt uit Wallonië.
mistakes.right: Zij leert Frans omdat haar man uit Wallonië komt.
mistakes.why: In the dependent clause the origin phrase comes before the finite verb.

mistakes.wrong: Zij leert Frans omdat haar man van Wallonië komt.
mistakes.right: Zij leert Frans omdat haar man uit Wallonië komt.
mistakes.why: For the place a person comes from, Dutch uses 'uit' (komen uit), not 'van'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat haar man uit Wallonië komt, leert zij Frans.
contrast.english: Because her husband comes from Wallonia, she is learning French.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'leert zij Frans'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The teacher being in traffic explains why the lesson starts late.

clauses.subject: De les
clauses.why: The subject comes first, so 'begint' is second; 'later' follows.

clauses.text: omdat de leraar in de file staat
clauses.subject: de leraar
clauses.why: The place phrase 'in de file' (in the traffic jam) stands before the finite verb 'staat', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-74.meaning: You say that the lesson starts later, because the teacher is stuck in traffic.
pat-omdat-74.order: The dependent clause ends with 'staat', behind 'in de file'. The verb 'staan' is used for being in a traffic jam (literally 'stands in the queue').
pat-omdat-74.forms: beginnen: de les begint. staan: de leraar staat. 'In de file staan' = to be in a traffic jam. 'File' is a de-word.
pat-omdat-74.compare: English 'is stuck in traffic' uses 'stuck'; Dutch says the teacher 'stands in the jam'. English keeps 'is' second; Dutch puts 'staat' last.

mistakes.wrong: De les begint later omdat de leraar staat in de file.
mistakes.right: De les begint later omdat de leraar in de file staat.
mistakes.why: The place phrase stands before the final verb.

mistakes.wrong: De les begint later omdat de leraar in de file is.
mistakes.right: De les begint later omdat de leraar in de file staat.
mistakes.why: Dutch uses 'staan' for being in a traffic jam, not 'zijn'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de leraar in de file staat, begint de les later.
contrast.english: Because the teacher is stuck in traffic, the lesson starts later.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'begint de les later'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: Her constant honesty is the ground for your trust.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'vertrouw' is second; 'haar' is the object pronoun.

clauses.subject: zij
clauses.why: 'Altijd eerlijk' (always honest) stands before the finite verb 'is', which closes the sentence.

pat-omdat-75.meaning: You say that you trust her because she is always honest.
pat-omdat-75.order: A short main clause is followed by a dependent clause where the adverb 'altijd' and the predicate 'eerlijk' come before 'is'. The sentence ends in the verb.
pat-omdat-75.forms: vertrouwen: ik vertrouw (inseparable prefix ver-). zijn: zij is. 'Haar' is the object form of 'zij'.
pat-omdat-75.compare: English 'because she is always honest' keeps 'is' before 'always honest'. Dutch moves it to the end.

mistakes.wrong: Ik vertrouw haar omdat zij is altijd eerlijk.
mistakes.right: Ik vertrouw haar omdat zij altijd eerlijk is.
mistakes.why: The finite verb goes to the end after omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Ik vertrouw haar omdat zij eerlijk altijd is.
mistakes.right: Ik vertrouw haar omdat zij altijd eerlijk is.
mistakes.why: The adverb 'altijd' comes before the predicate it modifies.

contrast.dutch: Omdat zij altijd eerlijk is, vertrouw ik haar.
contrast.english: Because she is always honest, I trust her.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'vertrouw ik haar'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The headache is the cause of the pill.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is first, so 'neemt' is second; 'een paracetamol' is the object.

clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: 'Hoofdpijn hebben' (to have a headache): the noun 'hoofdpijn' stands before the finite verb 'heeft'.

pat-omdat-76.meaning: You say that he takes a paracetamol because he has a headache.
pat-omdat-76.order: The two clauses both start with 'hij'. The dependent clause has the object 'hoofdpijn' before 'heeft'. Pain is expressed with 'hebben' and a noun, so no article is used.
pat-omdat-76.forms: nemen: hij neemt. hebben: hij heeft. 'Hoofdpijn hebben' = to have a headache. 'Paracetamol' takes 'een' here for one tablet.
pat-omdat-76.compare: English 'he has a headache' needs 'a'; Dutch 'hoofdpijn heeft' has none. English keeps 'has' before the object; Dutch puts it last.

mistakes.wrong: Hij neemt een paracetamol omdat hij heeft hoofdpijn.
mistakes.right: Hij neemt een paracetamol omdat hij hoofdpijn heeft.
mistakes.why: The finite verb goes behind the object in the dependent clause.

mistakes.wrong: Hij neemt een paracetamol omdat hij een hoofdpijn heeft.
mistakes.right: Hij neemt een paracetamol omdat hij hoofdpijn heeft.
mistakes.why: 'Hoofdpijn' is used without an article after hebben.

contrast.dutch: Omdat hij hoofdpijn heeft, neemt hij een paracetamol.
contrast.english: Because he has a headache, he is taking a paracetamol.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'neemt hij een paracetamol'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The need for new hardware is the reason for requesting a quote.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: Aanvragen (to request) is separable: 'vragen ... aan' wraps the object 'een offerte'.

clauses.text: omdat we een nieuwe server nodig hebben
clauses.subject: we
clauses.why: The object 'een nieuwe server' and the predicate 'nodig' come before the finite verb 'hebben', which closes the clause.

pat-omdat-77.meaning: You say that you are requesting a quote because you need a new server.
pat-omdat-77.order: The main clause splits aanvragen around its object. The dependent clause uses 'iets nodig hebben', with the object and 'nodig' before the finite 'hebben'.
pat-omdat-77.forms: aanvragen = aan + vragen: wij vragen aan. 'Een offerte' is a de-word. 'Nodig hebben' = to need. 'Een nieuwe server': -e after 'een' before a de-word.
pat-omdat-77.compare: English 'request a quote' has no particle; Dutch 'aanvragen' splits. English 'we need a new server' uses 'need'; Dutch says 'een nieuwe server nodig hebben'.

mistakes.wrong: We aanvragen een offerte omdat we een nieuwe server nodig hebben.
mistakes.right: We vragen een offerte aan omdat we een nieuwe server nodig hebben.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause; 'aan' goes last.

mistakes.wrong: We vragen een offerte aan omdat we hebben een nieuwe server nodig.
mistakes.right: We vragen een offerte aan omdat we een nieuwe server nodig hebben.
mistakes.why: After omdat the finite verb goes behind the object and 'nodig'.

contrast.dutch: Omdat we een nieuwe server nodig hebben, vragen we een offerte aan.
contrast.english: Because we need a new server, we are requesting a quote.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'vragen we ... aan'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The sudden stop is the reason for your check.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is first, so 'controleer' is second; 'de instellingen' is the plural object.

clauses.text: omdat de applicatie plots is gestopt
clauses.subject: de applicatie
clauses.why: The adverb 'plots' (suddenly) stands before the perfect group 'is gestopt', which closes the clause. Stoppen takes zijn when it means to come to a stop.

pat-omdat-78.meaning: You say that you check the settings because the application suddenly stopped.
pat-omdat-78.order: A short main clause, then a dependent clause that ends with the group 'is gestopt'. The adverb 'plots' stays in front of the group.
pat-omdat-78.forms: controleren: ik controleer. stoppen > gestopt; with zijn for 'to cease operating', with hebben for 'to stop something'. 'De instellingen' = the settings (plural).
pat-omdat-78.compare: English 'the application suddenly stopped' is a simple past. Dutch usually reports it with the perfect 'is gestopt'. English 'suddenly' stands before the verb, as 'plots' does here.

mistakes.wrong: Ik controleer de instellingen omdat is de applicatie plots gestopt.
mistakes.right: Ik controleer de instellingen omdat de applicatie plots is gestopt.
mistakes.why: After omdat the subject stands first; the verb group follows the adverb at the end of the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ik controleer de instellingen omdat de applicatie plots heeft gestopt.
mistakes.right: Ik controleer de instellingen omdat de applicatie plots is gestopt.
mistakes.why: When something comes to a stop by itself, stoppen takes zijn.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de applicatie plots is gestopt, controleer ik de instellingen.
contrast.english: Because the application suddenly stopped, I am checking the settings.
contrast.note: Reason first: the main clause inverts to 'controleer ik'.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want gives a reason, but it joins two main clauses, so the second clause keeps normal order.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'blijf' is second; 'thuis' follows it.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: After 'want' the second main clause keeps verb-second order: the subject 'ik' is first and 'ben' is second, not last.

pat-omdat-79.meaning: You say that you stay at home and add a reason as a second statement.
pat-omdat-79.order: Want is a coordinating word, like 'en' or 'maar': it does not change the order of the clause that follows. Compare 'omdat ik ziek ben', where the verb goes last. This card trains the choice between want and omdat.
pat-omdat-79.forms: blijven: ik blijf. zijn: ik ben. After want, 'ik ben ziek' keeps the verb in position two. Want is normally preceded by a comma.
pat-omdat-79.compare: English 'for' and 'because' both introduce a reason, but English does not change the verb position. Dutch does: omdat sends the verb to the end, want does not.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ziek ben.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben ziek.
mistakes.why: Want joins two main clauses, so the verb stays in position two. Sending 'ben' to the end is the pattern for omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Ik blijf thuis, want ben ik ziek.
mistakes.right: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben ziek.
mistakes.why: After want the subject comes first; there is no inversion because nothing has moved to the front.

contrast.dutch: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
contrast.english: I am staying at home because I am ill.
contrast.note: With omdat the second clause is dependent, so 'ben' moves to the end. The meaning is the same, but the word order differs.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want adds the reason as a second main clause, without changing its word order.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'nemen' is second; 'de bus' is its object.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: After 'want' the second main clause has the order 'het regent': subject, then the verb in second place. Here it looks the same as after omdat only because the clause has no other word.

pat-omdat-80.meaning: You say that you take the bus and give the reason as an extra statement.
pat-omdat-80.order: The second clause is a main clause, so its verb 'regent' is in position two. The order does not show the difference between want and omdat here; add one word and the difference appears: 'want het regent hard' versus 'omdat het hard regent'.
pat-omdat-80.forms: nemen: wij nemen. regenen: het regent. 'Want' always stands between two main clauses; it cannot start a sentence.
pat-omdat-80.compare: English 'for it is raining' sounds old-fashioned; Dutch 'want' is ordinary speech. English has no word-order change either way.

mistakes.wrong: We nemen de bus, want het hard regent.
mistakes.right: We nemen de bus, want het regent.
mistakes.why: Want does not send the verb to the end. 'Het hard regent' is the order after omdat, not after want, which keeps verb-second order: want het regent hard.

mistakes.wrong: We nemen de bus, want regent het.
mistakes.right: We nemen de bus, want het regent.
mistakes.why: Want does not cause inversion; the subject stays first.

contrast.dutch: We nemen de bus omdat het regent.
contrast.english: We take the bus because it is raining.
contrast.note: With omdat the clause becomes dependent; it looks identical here, but 'omdat het hard regent' would move the verb to the end.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want adds the reason as a second main clause: the speaker states the decision first, then the ground for it.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Ik is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'controleer' is second; 'de logs' is the object.

clauses.subject: de server
clauses.why: After 'want' the clause keeps verb-second order: the subject 'de server' is first and 'reageert' is second. 'Niet' follows the verb, it does not stand before it.

pat-omdat-81.meaning: You say that you are checking the logs and add why: the server does not respond.
pat-omdat-81.order: Compare this with 'omdat de server niet reageert': after omdat the verb 'reageert' moves behind 'niet'; after want it stays second and 'niet' follows it. One clause, two conjunctions, two orders.
pat-omdat-81.forms: controleren: ik controleer. reageren: de server reageert. Want needs a comma in front of it in writing. The negation 'niet' comes after the verb in a main clause.
pat-omdat-81.compare: English uses 'for' or 'because' without any change in word order. Dutch changes the order with omdat but not with want, so the learner has to choose the conjunction before the verb position is known.

mistakes.wrong: Ik controleer de logs, want de server niet reageert.
mistakes.right: Ik controleer de logs, want de server reageert niet.
mistakes.why: Want joins two main clauses, so 'reageert' stays second; 'niet reageert' is the pattern after omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Ik controleer de logs, want reageert de server niet.
mistakes.right: Ik controleer de logs, want de server reageert niet.
mistakes.why: Nothing is fronted after want, so the subject comes first.

contrast.dutch: Omdat de server niet reageert, controleer ik de logs.
contrast.english: Because the server is not responding, I am checking the logs.
contrast.note: With omdat in front, the dependent clause ends with 'reageert', and the main clause inverts to 'controleer ik'.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want explains her tiredness in a second main clause with a perfect tense.

clauses.subject: Zij
clauses.why: Zij is first, so 'is' is second; the predicate 'moe' follows.

clauses.subject: ze
clauses.why: After 'want' the order is normal: 'ze' first, 'heeft' second, and the participle 'geslapen' last. After omdat it would read 'ze weinig heeft geslapen'.

pat-omdat-82.meaning: You say that she is tired and add the reason: she slept little.
pat-omdat-82.order: The auxiliary 'heeft' is in position two of the second main clause and the participle 'geslapen' ends it, with 'weinig' in between. After want the clause has the same shape as a free-standing sentence.
pat-omdat-82.forms: slapen > geslapen (hebben). 'Heeft weinig geslapen' = slept little. 'Ze' and 'zij' are the same pronoun in two strengths.
pat-omdat-82.compare: English has 'for she slept little' in a literary register; Dutch 'want' is ordinary. In Dutch the verb positions tell you which conjunction was used.

mistakes.wrong: Zij is moe, want ze weinig heeft geslapen.
mistakes.right: Zij is moe, want ze heeft weinig geslapen.
mistakes.why: After want the finite verb stays in position two; the end-position order belongs to omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Zij is moe, want heeft ze weinig geslapen.
mistakes.right: Zij is moe, want ze heeft weinig geslapen.
mistakes.why: Want does not front anything, so the subject 'ze' comes before the verb.

contrast.dutch: Zij is moe omdat ze weinig heeft geslapen.
contrast.english: She is tired because she slept little.
contrast.note: With omdat the dependent clause ends with the group 'heeft geslapen'.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want gives the reason as a second main clause that contains a modal.

clauses.subject: Hij
clauses.why: Hij is the first constituent, so the finite verb 'komt' is second; 'later' follows it.

clauses.subject: hij
clauses.why: After 'want' the modal 'moet' is second and the infinitive 'werken' closes the clause, with 'nog' between them. After omdat it would be 'hij nog moet werken'.

pat-omdat-83.meaning: You say that he is coming later and add that he still has to work.
pat-omdat-83.order: Both clauses are main clauses with their own verb in position two. The second one, 'hij moet nog werken', shows modal plus infinitive in the normal main-clause order: the modal second, the infinitive last.
pat-omdat-83.forms: moeten: hij moet. werken: infinitive. 'Nog' = still. 'Want hij moet nog werken' versus 'omdat hij nog moet werken'.
pat-omdat-83.compare: English 'for he still has to work' uses 'has to'. Dutch uses the modal 'moet'. The English clause order never changes; Dutch moves the modal after omdat but not after want.

mistakes.wrong: Hij komt later, want hij nog moet werken.
mistakes.right: Hij komt later, want hij moet nog werken.
mistakes.why: After want the modal 'moet' stays in position two.

mistakes.wrong: Hij komt later, want moet hij nog werken.
mistakes.right: Hij komt later, want hij moet nog werken.
mistakes.why: Nothing precedes the subject after want, so there is no inversion.

contrast.dutch: Hij komt later omdat hij nog moet werken.
contrast.english: He is coming later because he still has to work.
contrast.note: With omdat the modal group 'moet werken' moves to the end of the dependent clause.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want supplies the reason you cannot talk now, as a spoken second sentence part.

clauses.subject: Ik
clauses.why: Terugbellen is separable: 'bel ... terug' around the object 'je'.

clauses.text: want ik zit nu in een vergadering
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: After 'want' the order is subject first and 'zit' second; 'nu' and 'in een vergadering' follow the verb. After omdat the verb 'zit' would be last.

pat-omdat-84.meaning: You say that you will call back, because you are in a meeting right now.
pat-omdat-84.order: The first clause splits the separable verb: bel ... terug. The second clause keeps 'zit' in position two. This is how a speaker quickly gives a reason on the phone.
pat-omdat-84.forms: terugbellen = terug + bellen. zitten: ik zit (to sit; 'in een vergadering zitten' = to be in a meeting). 'Nu' = now.
pat-omdat-84.compare: English 'I will call you back, as I am in a meeting' keeps the verb after the subject. In Dutch the position tells which conjunction you chose.

mistakes.wrong: Ik bel je terug, want ik nu in een vergadering zit.
mistakes.right: Ik bel je terug, want ik zit nu in een vergadering.
mistakes.why: After want the verb stays second; the verb-last order belongs to omdat.

mistakes.wrong: Ik terugbel je, want ik zit nu in een vergadering.
mistakes.right: Ik bel je terug, want ik zit nu in een vergadering.
mistakes.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: 'bel' second, 'terug' last.

contrast.dutch: Ik bel je terug omdat ik nu in een vergadering zit.
contrast.english: I will call you back because I am in a meeting now.
contrast.note: With omdat the dependent clause ends with 'zit', behind 'nu in een vergadering'.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want explains the closed shop with a short second main clause.

clauses.subject: De winkel
clauses.why: The subject comes first, so 'is' is second; 'dicht' is the predicate.

clauses.subject: het
clauses.why: After 'want' the clause keeps 'het is feestdag' in verb-second order. After omdat it would be 'het feestdag is'.

pat-omdat-85.meaning: You say that the shop is closed, and add: it is a public holiday.
pat-omdat-85.order: Both clauses have 'is' in position two. This pair is the easiest way to see what 'want' does: nothing. The second clause could stand alone as a sentence. The same words with omdat have 'is' last.
pat-omdat-85.forms: zijn: is in both clauses. 'Feestdag' is the predicate noun after 'is', without an article. 'Dicht' = closed.
pat-omdat-85.compare: English 'the shop is closed, for it is a holiday' does not change anything between the clauses. In Dutch the two 'is' forms keep the same position, which is exactly what marks 'want'.

mistakes.wrong: De winkel is dicht, want het feestdag is.
mistakes.right: De winkel is dicht, want het is feestdag.
mistakes.why: After want the verb stays second; it moves to the end only after omdat.

mistakes.wrong: De winkel is dicht, want is het feestdag.
mistakes.right: De winkel is dicht, want het is feestdag.
mistakes.why: No fronting after want: the subject 'het' comes first.

contrast.dutch: De winkel is dicht omdat het feestdag is.
contrast.english: The shop is closed because it is a public holiday.
contrast.note: With omdat the dependent clause has 'is' at the end.

sense.label: want = for/because (coordinating)
sense.why: Want gives the reason for the wait in a clause that keeps main-clause order.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so 'wachten' is second; 'even' (for a moment) follows.

clauses.text: want de dokter is nog bezig
clauses.subject: de dokter
clauses.why: After 'want' the order is subject, then 'is' in second place, then 'nog bezig'. After omdat the verb 'is' would close the clause.

pat-omdat-86.meaning: You say that you are waiting a moment, because the doctor is still busy.
pat-omdat-86.order: The second clause is a normal statement. Compare 'omdat de dokter nog bezig is': there the whole group 'nog bezig is' is at the end. With want, 'is' stays directly after the subject.
pat-omdat-86.forms: wachten: wij wachten. zijn: de dokter is. 'Even' = for a moment. 'Bezig zijn' = to be busy.
pat-omdat-86.compare: English 'for the doctor is still busy' keeps order. Dutch 'want' also keeps order, whereas 'omdat' changes it.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten even, want de dokter nog bezig is.
mistakes.right: We wachten even, want de dokter is nog bezig.
mistakes.why: After want the finite verb 'is' stays in position two; omdat would send it to the end.

mistakes.wrong: We wachten even, want is de dokter nog bezig.
mistakes.right: We wachten even, want de dokter is nog bezig.
mistakes.why: No inversion after want: the subject comes first.

contrast.dutch: We wachten even omdat de dokter nog bezig is.
contrast.english: We are waiting a moment because the doctor is still busy.
contrast.note: With omdat the verb 'is' moves to the end of the dependent clause.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The passed test is the condition-turned-cause that lets installation start.

clauses.subject: de test
clauses.why: 'Is geslaagd' is the group (zijn plus participle) at the end. Slagen forms its perfect with zijn.

clauses.subject: de installatie
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so the modal 'kan' comes before its noun-phrase subject 'de installatie'. The infinitive 'beginnen' closes the clause.

pat-omdat-87.meaning: You say that the installation can now start, because the test has passed.
pat-omdat-87.order: After the fronted reason the modal comes second, before the whole subject phrase 'de installatie', and the infinitive ends the sentence. The structure 'kan + noun phrase + infinitive' is typical of inversion with a modal.
pat-omdat-87.forms: slagen > geslaagd (zijn). kunnen: de installatie kan. beginnen: infinitive after the modal. 'Geslaagd' also means 'succeeded'.
pat-omdat-87.compare: English 'the installation can begin' keeps the subject before 'can'; Dutch has 'kan de installatie beginnen' after the front clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de test is geslaagd, de installatie kan beginnen.
mistakes.right: Omdat de test is geslaagd, kan de installatie beginnen.
mistakes.why: Behind the fronted test clause the modal 'kan' must precede the noun phrase 'de installatie'.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat de test heeft geslaagd, kan de installatie beginnen.
mistakes.right: Omdat de test is geslaagd, kan de installatie beginnen.
mistakes.why: Slagen forms its perfect tense with zijn, so the auxiliary is 'is'; 'heeft geslaagd' is not used.

contrast.dutch: De installatie kan beginnen omdat de test is geslaagd.
contrast.english: The installation can begin because the test has passed.
contrast.note: Main clause first: the noun-phrase subject opens the sentence, so the modal 'kan' is simply second.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The recent move is the reason you do not know the area.

clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: 'Net' (just) stands before the participle 'verhuisd', and 'ben' closes the clause. Verhuizen takes zijn.

clauses.text: ken ik de buurt nog niet goed
clauses.subject: ik
clauses.why: The omdat-clause is position one, so 'ken' precedes 'ik'. 'Nog niet goed' (not yet well) follows the object 'de buurt'.

pat-omdat-88.meaning: You say that you do not know the neighbourhood well yet, because you have only just moved.
pat-omdat-88.order: The recent past ('net verhuisd ben') comes first as the reason. The main clause inverts to 'ken ik' and ends with the adverb phrase 'nog niet goed'.
pat-omdat-88.forms: verhuizen > verhuisd (zijn). kennen: ik ken. 'De buurt' = the neighbourhood. 'Net' (just) marks something that happened a moment ago.
pat-omdat-88.compare: English 'because I have only just moved' uses 'only just'; Dutch uses 'net'. English 'I do not know' needs 'do not'; Dutch puts 'nog niet goed' after the object.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik net verhuisd ben, ik ken de buurt nog niet goed.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik net verhuisd ben, ken ik de buurt nog niet goed.
mistakes.why: The main verb is second after the fronted clause.

mistakes.wrong: Omdat ik net ben verhuisd, ken ik de buurt nog niet goed.
mistakes.right: Omdat ik net verhuisd ben, ken ik de buurt nog niet goed.
mistakes.why: This card keeps the participle before the auxiliary; both orders are heard in practice, but not 'ben' before 'net'.

contrast.dutch: Ik ken de buurt nog niet goed omdat ik net verhuisd ben.
contrast.english: I do not know the neighbourhood well yet because I have only just moved.
contrast.note: Main clause first: subject-first 'Ik ken'.

sense.label: omdat = because
sense.why: The accident is the cause of the new route.

clauses.subject: We
clauses.why: We is first, so 'gebruiken' is second; 'een andere route' is the object.

clauses.text: omdat er een ongeluk is gebeurd
clauses.subject: een ongeluk
